heading: In one minute
text: A new game program, not a mod. Horizon is written from scratch in Rust. It reads the same worlds, plays by the same rules and generates the same terrain as the Java game. Checked against vanilla. 281 automated tests ("harnesses") feed the same inputs to Horizon and to the real game, then compare the results. Today every subsystem matches in every harness that compares it. That is 100% of what the harnesses compare, which is not proof that nothing else differs. The status table lists what is covered. Light and fast. It starts quickly, uses little memory and draws efficiently. See Performance for what is measured and what is not. A few things vanilla doesn't have. Its own settings, added to vanilla's menus the way mods add theirs, graphics presets, distant terrain, controller support, optional extras such as dynamic lights, official mods such as zoom and a minimap, an invite code to play your world with friends, and a server you can run without Java.

heading: What Horizon is not
text: Not Minecraft itself. Horizon contains no Minecraft code, assets or data, and it never downloads them. You need your own legally obtained copy of Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3. Horizon builds its game files from that copy, on your computer. Not a place where Java mods run. Forge, NeoForge, Fabric and Quilt mod jars do not work in Horizon, and neither do Mixins. Horizon has its own mod system, and the launcher can port some Java mods' content. See Mods and data packs and Modpacks . Not for other versions. Horizon plays Java Edition 26.3. Worlds from older versions (1.8 to 26.2) are upgraded the way vanilla upgrades them. Not an official Minecraft product. It is not approved by or associated with Mojang or Microsoft. Not able to sign in to a Microsoft account yet. Until it can, Horizon cannot join servers that check accounts. See Multiplayer .

heading: Supported systems
text: Linux, x86-64. A graphics card with Vulkan drivers. Builds are made on Ubuntu 22.04, so use a distribution at least that recent. macOS, Apple Silicon. Any M1 or newer, on macOS 11 or later. Windows, x64. Vulkan or DirectX 12. Horizon picks DirectX 12 by itself when Vulkan does not work. There is no build for Intel Macs, 32-bit systems, or ARM Linux and Windows. The server can be built from source on other systems.

heading: Where to go next
text: Playing: install and first launch , settings worth knowing , multiplayer and what to do when something breaks . Hosting: host a server , from the launcher or the command line. Going further: modpacks , mods and data packs and performance . Making mods: make a mod , content or native, from the first file to the registry. Helping out: contribute and the FAQ .

heading: What you need
text: Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3, played once. Install it with the official Minecraft launcher (or Prism Launcher, MultiMC, the Modrinth App, ATLauncher or GDLauncher) and start 26.3 once, so it downloads its files. Horizon reads them from there and never copies them anywhere else. Java 25, a JDK , for the one-time preparation only (the game itself needs no Java). Nothing to install: the launcher uses the Java the Minecraft launcher downloaded for 26.3, or downloads that same Java from Mojang. A JDK you installed yourself (for example Eclipse Temurin 25 ) works too. A computer on the supported list . On Linux and Windows that means a graphics card with Vulkan (or DirectX 12 on Windows).

heading: Download the launcher
text: Get the newest launcher from the Download button on the home page , which picks the right file for your system, or from the launcher releases on GitHub . Linux: download horizon-launcher-linux-x86_64.tar.gz , extract it and run horizon-launcher . macOS: download horizon-launcher-macos-arm64.dmg , open it and drag Horizon onto Applications. The first time, macOS says it cannot check the app, because it is not signed with a paid Apple developer account. On macOS 14 and earlier, right-click Horizon, choose Open , then Open again. On macOS 15 and later, open it once, then go to System Settings, Privacy & Security and choose Open Anyway . After that it opens normally. Windows: download horizon-launcher-windows-x64.zip , extract it and run horizon-launcher.exe . Every release also carries SHA256SUMS and a signature, SHA256SUMS.sig , if you want to check your download. The launcher does not check that signature for you yet.

heading: First launch
text: Open the launcher. On the Play page, if it says "No version installed yet", choose Choose a version . On the Versions page, install the newest one. The launcher installs it in its own folder. Back on Play , the launcher says "Not prepared. Horizon needs the files of your own Minecraft 26.3." Choose Prepare . It finds your Minecraft folder by itself in the usual places. If it cannot, it lists where it looked, and Choose… next to the Minecraft folder lets you point it at yours. Wait a few minutes. When it says "Prepared for Minecraft 26.3", choose Play . The game opens on vanilla's title screen. Your worlds, options and logs live in the game folder, which is not inside a version's folder, so updating or removing a version never touches them: Linux: ~/.local/share/horizon macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/horizon Windows: %APPDATA%\horizon No Microsoft sign-in yet. The launcher's Settings page has an Accounts section, but signing in with a Microsoft account does not work for players today. It needs an app registration and an approval from Mojang that the project does not have yet. You do not need an account to play single player.

heading: Updating
text: Horizon. The launcher looks for a new Nightly when it starts and every 30 minutes while it is open. With Install new versions automatically on (the default), it installs it and moves you to it if you were on the newest version. Your worlds stay where they are. New Nightlies come out a few times a day; an older Nightly is removed once nothing plays it, and versions you installed by hand stay until you remove them on the Versions page. The launcher. It updates itself from its own releases, then shows Restart in its footer. A launcher from before 0.2 (0.16 or older) updates twice in a row: first to 0.17, then to 0.2. Then it installs Horizon 0.2 like any update.

heading: One version for everyone: the Nightly
text: Horizon ships one build, the Nightly : the latest Horizon, plus a few changes the Team picked to try before they are merged. Before a Nightly goes out, the game has to start and draw a world on our test machine, and nothing goes out while a serious problem is open. The game shows which Nightly you play ("Nightly 2026-10-28 · 9b772b2"): give that when you report a bug. You can install an earlier one (the last week's) or an older numbered release by hand on the Versions page. Launchers from before this change still show a Nightly builds setting, or an Updates choice. The launcher updates itself, and from then on it plays the Nightly for everyone; the setting goes away.

heading: The Versions page
text: It lists Horizon's builds, newest first: the current Nightly, the last week's, then the numbered releases from before. You can install a version, remove it, or choose which one Play starts. Each release's notes are on the Patch notes page, and on GitHub .

heading: Something went wrong
text: See Logs, crashes and bug reports .

heading: Who builds it
text: Horizon is Ludovic Marie's project: he decides what it does and what ships. Most of the code is written by AI agents : Claude sessions that Ludovic runs, and contributors' own AI tools. Some contributors write their code by hand. Agents say what they are. A pull request opened by one of Ludovic's agents starts with "Opened by Ludovic's AI agent (Claude), not by Ludovic himself.", its comments start with "🤖 Agent:", and its commits name the agent in a Co-Authored-By line.

heading: How changes are checked
text: Not every line is read by a person. Instead, every change is checked against the real game, automatically: Harnesses. A harness is a test that gives the same inputs to Horizon and to the real Minecraft 26.3, then compares the results. There are 326 of them (25 October 2026), from world generation to mobs, redstone and commands. The status table shows what they cover. Passing them all does not prove that nothing else differs. Checks on every pull request. verify runs on GitHub's machines for every pull request and every change to main: formatting, lints with warnings treated as errors, the tests, and the check that no Minecraft files are committed. Main takes no change without it. parity runs the harnesses a change can affect, on a machine that holds a copy of Minecraft. For a pull request from a fork, it runs once a maintainer has read the change. Outside contributions are checked again. Before a contributor's pull request merges, Ludovic's agents compare what it claims with vanilla's own code, review it line by line, rewrite the weak parts, and test it in single player, on a LAN and on a dedicated server where those apply. Releases are tested first. A release is published only after its smoke test passes (the game starts and draws a world) and while no issue is labelled release-blocker .

heading: Why it's safe to run
text: Open source. All of the code is public on GitHub , under the MIT licence. Built from the public code. Releases are built by GitHub Actions, the build service of GitHub, from the public source. Linux and Windows are built on GitHub's machines, and macOS on Ludovic's Mac mini, which runs GitHub Actions jobs. Every build log is public . Signed checksums. Every release has a SHA256SUMS file, a fingerprint of each download, and SHA256SUMS.sig , a signature of that list made with Horizon's release key, which only release builds from main can use. The launcher and horizon-server update check both before they install anything, and refuse a file that does not match. The very first server install with install.sh checks the fingerprint but not the signature. Not yet signed by Apple or Microsoft. The macOS app is not notarized by Apple, because it is not signed with a paid Apple developer account, so macOS asks you to confirm the first time ( Install shows how). The Windows programs are not code-signed either, so Windows may warn you too. Mods are off until you choose them. A content mod is data only: blocks, items, recipes, textures. A native mod is code with your rights on the computer, so the launcher builds it only after a warning that names it, into a game of its own with its own worlds, and the registry lists one only after a maintainer has read its source. See Mods and data packs . Nothing collected unless you say yes. Data collection is off until you turn it on, with four separate switches. The one exception is an anonymous "I'm playing" ping for the launcher's player count, which holds nothing about you. See Privacy .

heading: What it doesn't contain
text: No Minecraft files. Horizon contains no Minecraft code, assets or data, and never downloads them. The launcher builds the game files on your computer from your own copy of Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3. A check that runs on every pull request ( tools/check_public_tree.py ) keeps game files and decompiled code out of the repository and its history. No code from other mods. Since 24 October 2026, Horizon's code may only be written from Minecraft 26.3 itself and public documentation, never from another mod, loader or renderer ( the rule ). That day shader packs were removed ( #1561 ), after a developer of Iris showed that our shader pack code had been written from Iris's source. They are being written again from a description of the pack format only.

heading: Check it yourself
text: Read the code and its checks. The source , the checks on every pull request and the release builds . Compare the fingerprints. Put a release's files and its SHA256SUMS in one folder and run sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing (on macOS shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing , on Windows Get-FileHash <file> in PowerShell). Each file should say OK . Check the signature. Download a whole release into a folder, then from a clone of the repository run cargo run -p horizon-release-sign -- verify --tag <tag> <folder> . The public key is in crates/horizon-release-sign/release-keys.txt . Build it yourself. The README explains how to build from source .

heading: Settings worth knowing
text: Horizon plays like vanilla out of the box. This page covers the settings that are different or new: graphics, distant terrain, resource packs, controllers and a few optional extras. The game's menus are vanilla's. Horizon adds its own settings to vanilla's Options screen the way mods do: Horizon Settings... and Mods... take the last two buttons of the grid. Horizon Settings opens Graphics, Advanced Graphics, Controller Settings, Extras and Mods, each a screen of vanilla's buttons and sliders. The graphics buttons are also at the top of Video Settings , and Controller Settings at the bottom of Controls . Video Settings, with Horizon's graphics buttons at the top

heading: Graphics: presets, Simple and Advanced
text: Options, Video Settings starts with Horizon Graphics... and Advanced Graphics... (also in Options, Horizon Settings ). Horizon Graphics has a preset (Performance, Balanced, Quality, Ultra or Custom) and LOD distance. Advanced Graphics has every Horizon setting, in groups: Rendering, Quality, Display, Preferences, Performance and Overlay. Vanilla's own settings (render distance, field of view, frame rate, VSync, GUI scale and the rest) stay on Video Settings, where vanilla has them. Every row has a one-line description and its cost in frame time: none, low, medium or high. Changes apply at once, except worker threads, which apply at the next start. A preset sets the quality settings together, and changing one of them turns the preset into Custom . Two settings are worth knowing on laptops and handhelds. Battery mode (Performance group, off by default) caps the frame rate at 60 in a world and 30 in menus, and uses half the automatic worker threads. The performance overlay (Overlay group) shows the frame rate, frame times and a graph over the game. Not available: anisotropic filtering, MSAA (FXAA is there instead) and exclusive fullscreen (fullscreen is borderless).

heading: Distant terrain (LOD)
text: LOD Distance draws far-away terrain as simplified columns, so you can see much farther than the render distance. It is off by default . Turn it on in the Video settings and choose 64, 128, 256, 512 or 1024 chunks. Keep the normal render distance modest next to it. For example 12 chunks with a LOD distance of 256. Full Detail Distance sets the nearby range. LOD does not raise the simulation distance: far terrain is only drawn, not simulated. Detail arrives gradually. A big radius does not mean everything is drawn right away. Far terrain is made from the world's seed, so places you have not visited are drawn too, close to what they will be. Small features, fluid edges and lighting can differ from the real chunks. Horizon caps far terrain on integrated graphics and holds it back on computers with four threads.

heading: Graphics API on Windows
text: Linux always uses Vulkan and macOS always uses Metal. On Windows there is a choice, in Options, Video Settings, Advanced Graphics, Performance, Graphics API : Auto (the default) uses Vulkan, and DirectX 12 when Vulkan has no graphics card or driver that works. Vulkan and DirectX 12 force one of the two. The change applies at the next start. If Vulkan gives you trouble, try DirectX 12.

heading: Shader packs
text: Shader packs have been removed for now. They will come back later, written again from scratch. Packs in your shaderpacks folder are left where they are.

heading: Resource packs
text: Java Edition resource packs work. Put the folder or .zip in the resourcepacks folder of the game folder and pick it on the Resource Packs screen, which is vanilla's screen. The game reloads every loader from the pack, as vanilla does. The launcher's Mods page can download them from Modrinth (see Mods and data packs ). Resource packs: what works lists everything a 26.3 resource pack can change and whether Horizon honours it.

heading: Controllers
text: Horizon plays with PlayStation (DualShock 4 and DualSense), Xbox (360, One and Series) and Nintendo Switch Pro controllers, and with the Steam Deck's built-in controls. Vanilla has no controller support at all, so this is Horizon's own. With no controller connected, nothing changes. Settings are in Options, Controls, Controller Settings (or Options, Horizon Settings, Controller Settings ): on or off, vibration, look sensitivity, inverting the axes, deadzones, button glyphs and remapping. Menus, the inventory and chat work with a controller, with an on-screen keyboard for text. On a DualSense you can also set adaptive triggers and the lightbar. On the Steam Deck, Steam's default layout works with no setup.

heading: Extras
text: Options, Horizon Settings, Extras holds small, optional conveniences. Every one is off by default, so a fresh install behaves like vanilla: fullbright, auto-reconnect, Mouse Tweaks-style inventory controls and inventory sorting. The FPS counter, the keystroke display, zoom and the minimap are official mods now, in Options, Mods : if you had one on, the game installed it for you on its first start after the update, with your settings. One more is dynamic lights : a torch, lantern or other light source that you hold, that lies dropped as an item, or a burning mob, lights the blocks around it. It is client-side only, so other players do not see it.

heading: Where your settings are stored
text: In the game folder, next to options.txt . That file keeps vanilla's own keys and values, so a vanilla client can share the folder. Horizon's own settings are in horizon-graphics.txt , horizon-controller.txt and a few more beside it.

heading: Play with friends from your own world
text: This needs no server and no account. In your world, open the pause menu and choose the Friends button (the icon with two people), then Start Sharing . Horizon opens the world to your network and shows an invite code with Copy Code . Send the code to your friends. On their side, your friends choose the Friends button on the title screen (or Join a friend on the launcher's Play page), paste the code and choose Join . Pasting the code in Direct Connection works too. There is no Horizon server in the middle. The code holds the host's addresses and a secret key, and the game between you is encrypted with it. A code works for as long as you keep sharing: closing the world or quitting ends it. Can your friends reach you? The Play with Friends screen says what the game found: On the same network, or over a VPN such as Tailscale or ZeroTier, it just works. Over the internet, it asks your router to open the port by itself (UPnP). If the router does not allow it, forward TCP port 25580 to your computer. Some internet providers share one address between many homes (CGNAT), and no port can be opened. Use a VPN such as Tailscale instead; the code already contains your VPN address. Guests join with the name their game uses. There is no account check, so only share the code with people you trust. Guests can also use the host's workstations: the crafter, loom, stonecutter, grindstone, anvil, smithing table, enchanting table, beacon, lectern and cartography table.

heading: Open to LAN
text: As in vanilla, Open to LAN in the pause menu lets people on the same network join your world. They see it in their server list. A vanilla 26.3 client can join a Horizon LAN world, and Horizon can join a vanilla one. LAN worlds are in offline mode.

heading: Joining a server
text: The Multiplayer page works like vanilla's: Add server saves one, Direct connect takes an address, and your servers are listed with their message of the day and ping. Horizon joins vanilla 26.3 servers and Horizon's own. Online mode. Most public servers run in online mode: they check that each player really owns Minecraft by asking Mojang. To pass that check, the game needs a Microsoft account sign-in, and Horizon cannot do that yet. It needs an app registration and an approval from Mojang that the project does not have. So today: Horizon can join servers in offline mode only ( online-mode=false ): your own, a friend's, or a server on your network or a VPN. It cannot join servers that check accounts. That is most public servers, and Realms. Skins served over https show the default skin unless they were already cached. Anyone can join an offline server under any name, so run one only on your network or a VPN, or share it with people you trust. Host a server explains the details.

heading: Vanilla players on a Horizon server
text: A vanilla 26.3 client can join a Horizon server, and in online mode it signs in with its own account as on a vanilla server. Secure chat works for those players.

heading: If the game crashes
text: The launcher notices. It shows what went wrong, in one line, with buttons: Open report opens the crash report. Copy report copies it, so you can paste it where you report the bug. Open logs folder opens the folder with the logs and crash reports. Report on Discord takes you to our Discord server.

heading: Where the files are
text: Everything is in the game folder, which is the same for every version you install: Linux: ~/.local/share/horizon macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/horizon Windows: %APPDATA%\horizon Inside it: logs/latest.log is the log of the current or last run. Older runs are kept as logs/<date>-<number>.log.gz . crash-reports/crash-<date>_<time>-client.txt is written when the game crashes. It holds the error, where it happened, your computer, your graphics card, your render settings, your resource packs and the last 50 lines of the log. The launcher's Settings page has a Logs row with an Open button. On the command line, horizon-launcher logs --crash prints the newest crash report and horizon-launcher logs --lines 200 the end of the log.

heading: What to try first
text: The game does not start, or crashes straight away. Update the launcher and Horizon, and your graphics drivers. On Windows, try Graphics API: DirectX 12 (see Settings ). "Not prepared" or "Minecraft 26.3 was not found". Sign in with a Microsoft account that owns Java Edition and press Play: with no Minecraft installed, the launcher downloads 26.3 from Mojang for your account and prepares it. To use an install you already have, point the launcher at your Minecraft folder ( Choose… next to Minecraft folder on the Play page), then choose Prepare again. Preparation says Java 25 is needed. Update the launcher: it then uses the Java the Minecraft launcher downloaded for 26.3, or downloads it from Mojang. If it still can't (no internet, say), install a Java 25 JDK, for example Eclipse Temurin 25. Slow or stuttering. Lower the render distance, turn LOD off, or pick the Performance preset. The performance overlay (Video, Advanced, Overlay) shows what is slow. A resource pack broke something. Switch it off, or take it out of its folder.

heading: Reporting a bug
text: Good places, in this order: GitHub issues: github.com/horizon-rust/horizon/issues . Search first; someone may have reported it already. Discord: the bugs channel on our Discord server , if you would rather talk it through. Include: what you did and what you expected; your Horizon version (shown on the launcher's Play page) and the launcher's version; your system and graphics card; the crash report, or the end of latest.log , if there is one. Read it first: logs can hold your player name and server addresses, and lines of chat. A Horizon bug is any place where it differs from vanilla 26.3, so "vanilla does X and Horizon does Y" is the best report there is.

heading: Data the launcher can send
text: The launcher can send performance statistics, crash reports, bug reports and benchmarks, but only the kinds you allow, and everything is off until you say yes. See Privacy for what is sent, how long it is kept and how to delete it.

heading: Host a server
text: horizon-server runs a Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3 server with Horizon's own game as the engine. It is one native program: no Java, one settings file, a web panel and backups. Vanilla 26.3 clients and Horizon clients can join it. There are two ways to run one. The launcher's Servers page does everything with buttons and no commands. The command line is for a VPS or a headless machine. Both run the same program and keep the same folder. The Servers page is in the launcher since version 0.15. The launcher updates itself, so open it once to get it.

heading: Before you start
text: You need your own copy of Minecraft 26.3 , like for playing: the server reads its game files from the ones you prepared. See Install . Horizon players cannot join servers that check accounts yet. That needs a Microsoft sign-in, which Horizon does not have. So a server for Horizon players runs in offline mode, which means anyone who can reach it can join under any name. Keep it on your network or a VPN such as Tailscale, and use a whitelist ("Friends only" in the launcher). Vanilla players can join an offline server too. A server that checks accounts is fine for vanilla players. It works as on a vanilla server, and Horizon players cannot join it yet. Nothing of Mojang's is downloaded or shipped with the server.

heading: From the launcher: the Servers page
text: Servers is in the launcher's top navigation, between Modpacks and Patch notes . The Play page also has a Host a server button that leads there.

heading: Create a server
text: Choose Create a server . To use a server folder you already have, choose Add a server folder… instead. The dialog asks for: Name . World: New world (with an optional seed) or Copy one of my worlds . Game mode: Survival , Creative or Adventure . Difficulty: Peaceful , Easy , Normal or Hard . Most players at once: use – and + . Who can join: Friends only or Anyone with the address . With Friends only, type your friends' names; the first one becomes an operator. Check Minecraft accounts , off by default. Leave it off for Horizon players. Turn it on only if every player signs in with Microsoft. I agree to the Minecraft EULA , with a Read it link. You must tick it. Everything has a default, so ticking the EULA and choosing Create makes a friends-only survival world. You can change all of it later. The Create a server dialog

heading: Start it and watch it
text: Open the server with Open on its row. At the top, a line says whether it is Stopped, Starting, Running, Restarting, Stopping or Updating, with how long it has been up. Then: Start and Stop , and Restart . Open the web panel and Open the folder . Four tiles: Players online , TPS (20 is full speed), MSPT (how long a tick takes) and RAM . Four tabs: Overview , Players , Settings and Backups . The Overview tab has the server's console, with a command line: type a command and press Enter. If the game crashes, the launcher restarts it by itself and says so ("The game crashed N times and was restarted by itself"). A running server's page in the launcher

heading: Let your friends join
text: The Overview tab shows Address on this network with a Copy button. Friends on the same Wi-Fi choose Multiplayer, Add server and paste it. For friends elsewhere, the page offers Friends over the internet through Tailscale , which is free, needs nothing changed on your router and reaches only the people you invite. Depending on what it finds, it shows: Install Tailscale if it is not installed, Open Tailscale if it is not running, or Sign in to Tailscale if you are signed out. Each has Check again . Once it runs, the server's Tailscale name with Copy . Friends type it in Multiplayer, once they have accepted your invitation. Invite a friend: open Tailscale's admin console, or Use an access token… so the launcher can make the invitation itself. Type their email (optional), choose Make an invitation and send them the link. The list shows Withdraw for an invitation not accepted yet and Stop sharing for one that was. Limit them to Minecraft changes your Tailscale access controls so invited friends reach the server and nothing else on your computer. Remove the limit undoes it. Horizon never turns on Tailscale Funnel: the server is not put on the public internet. The other way is to forward TCP port 25565 on your router to the computer. Inviting a friend through Tailscale

heading: Players
text: The Players tab lists who is Online now , with Make operator (or Remove operator ), Kick and Ban . Under Who may join , the Friends only switch turns the whitelist on. Type a player's name and choose Let in to add them.

heading: Settings
text: The Settings tab has the message in the server list, game mode, difficulty, PvP, most players at once, view distance, simulation distance, port, Check Minecraft accounts and Run in the background and at login . Each says whether it applies at once or after a restart, and the page then offers Restart now . A value the server would refuse shows in red under its field. When something is wrong the launcher says so in plain words. If it can fix it, there is a button: Use port 25566 when the port is busy, Prepare the game files when they are missing.

heading: Backups and updates
text: The Backups tab has Back up now , and Back up automatically (every 6 hours, keeping the last 12; backups you make by hand are never deleted). Restore next to a backup asks you to confirm with Replace the world , and keeps the world it replaces. Under This server's Horizon , Check for updates and Update now move the server to the newest release. The world is backed up first, and the server goes back to the old release by itself if the new one does not start. A server's Backups tab

heading: From the command line
text: This works today, on a VPS or any computer. Everything below is the same program the launcher runs.

heading: 1. Install
text: On Linux (x86-64) and macOS (Apple Silicon): curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/horizon-rust/horizon/main/packaging/server/install.sh | sh On Windows (x64), in PowerShell: irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/horizon-rust/horizon/main/packaging/server/install.ps1 | iex The script downloads the latest release from GitHub, checks it against the SHA-256 GitHub publishes, and never asks for sudo or administrator rights. It puts horizon-server and horizon-prepare in ~/.local/bin (on Windows, in your PATH). Other systems, such as Linux on ARM, build from source.

heading: 2. Prepare the game files
text: You need Minecraft 26.3 played once, Java 25 (a JDK) and the 26.3 server.jar , which is the downloads.server.url in your launcher's versions/26.3/26.3.json . Then: horizon-prepare --prepare --server-jar /path/to/server.jar On a machine with no Minecraft , prepare on your own computer (with the launcher or horizon-prepare ) and copy the prepared 26.3 folder to the server, into ~/.local/share/horizon/game-files/horizon-client/26.3 .

heading: 3. First run
text: mkdir my-server && cd my-server horizon-server init horizon-server start horizon-server status init asks whether you accept the Minecraft EULA , the world's name and seed, the port, whether to use a whitelist and who to add, and whether to make the first player an operator. It writes server.toml . Every question has a flag, so it also runs from a script. Players join at your computer's address and the port, 25565 by default. horizon-server run runs in the foreground with the console on your terminal instead.

heading: 4. The everyday commands
text: horizon-server run in the foreground, with the console horizon-server start | stop | restart in the background horizon-server status up or not, TPS, MSPT, players, RAM horizon-server cmd COMMAND... one console command, and its answer horizon-server logs [-f] [-n N] the log; -f follows it horizon-server op NAME | deop NAME horizon-server whitelist add|remove NAME horizon-server backup | backups | restore BACKUP horizon-server panel a one-time login link for the web panel horizon-server service install start it with the computer horizon-server update [--check] install the newest release and restart on it horizon-server rollback back to the release before Settings are in server.toml : the message of the day, port, most players, online mode, whitelist, view distance, game mode, difficulty, backups and the panel. Changes apply at the next restart. A vanilla server folder works as it is: run horizon-server init in it, and the world, ops.json and the whitelist keep vanilla's names and formats. The server restarts the game by itself if it crashes. Updates never happen on their own: it tells you a new release is out, and horizon-server update backs up the world, switches, and goes back by itself if the new game does not start.

heading: The web panel
text: horizon-server panel prints a login link that works once, for ten minutes. The panel shows live TPS, MSPT, RAM and CPU for the last ten minutes, the players (with a kick button), the console, the backups, and Restart and Stop. It listens on this computer only. To reach it from elsewhere, put your Tailscale address in [panel] bind , or forward the port over SSH. Never put it on the open internet.

heading: What does not work yet
text: Horizon players cannot join a server that checks accounts (see above). No Docker image is published. You can build one from the repository. Settings in server.toml apply at the next restart, not live. console (attach to a server running in the background) and ban and pardon as their own commands are coming. In the meantime, horizon-server cmd ban NAME works. The full reference, with every option, is docs/hosting.md in the repository, and docs/server.md explains the design.

heading: How fast is it
text: On the latest bot benchmark, with up to 50 players, Horizon used 3.8 to 4.8 times less memory than vanilla, Paper and Fabric with Lithium, started in about 8 seconds against 15 to 22, and used the least CPU from 10 players up. Its average tick was longer than Paper's at low player counts. See Performance for the numbers and what they mean.

heading: Modpacks
text: Java mod jars do not run in Horizon. Instead, the launcher reads a modpack, tells you which of its mods Horizon can carry over, and brings over the ones it can. This page explains what that means today and where the limits are. Early. The Modpacks page works, but no large pack runs as a whole in Horizon yet. What carries over today is mods made of data and assets: blocks, items, recipes, loot tables, tags, models, textures and structures. Mods with Java code do not, yet.

heading: What the Modpacks page does
text: Open Modpacks in the launcher. (From the next launcher release, it is the Modpacks tab of the Mods page.) Import a pack. Choose Import a pack file… for a Modrinth .mrpack or a CurseForge zip, or Import an instance folder… for a Prism, MultiMC or CurseForge instance. The Mods page can also find a Modrinth modpack and import it for you (see Mods and data packs ). From the next launcher release it also ports it in the same step, so you can press Play right away. Read the coverage report. For every mod in the pack it says Ported , Partial , Not yet or Not needed , with the reason. You can filter the list by status. Port. Port N mods gets the jars of the mods this computer can carry over today, and carries them over for the version you picked. It copies the jars from a folder you have, or downloads them from the pack's own links (or the same file from Modrinth's download network), and checks their hashes. CurseForge downloads are coming soon, so for files that only CurseForge has, choose Use jars from my instance… and point it at your installed instance. Play. Play with N mods starts the game as the pack's own profile, with its own saves and options, and those mods on. Nothing is uploaded or shared. The mod jars and what is made from them stay on your computer.

heading: What carries over, and what does not
text: Carries over today: content mods whose substance is data and assets. Blocks and items built on vanilla's shapes, recipes, loot tables, tags, models, textures and language files, and structures that are described in data, such as the structure mods that use jigsaw pools. Loot tables and structures from the mods you carry show up in your world. Not yet: Mods with Java code: machines, magic, new mob behaviour, anything that needs the mod's own logic. Each of these must be ported by hand as a Horizon native mod , and checked against the original mod running in a Java test instance. That work is under way; none of it is something you can install yet. World generation written in code: custom biomes, terrain shaping and structure types that are Java classes. Scripts such as KubeJS, and recipe viewers and map mods that are built around Java. Not needed: performance mods such as Sodium, Lithium or FerriteCore (Horizon is the replacement), and libraries whose job is to give mods a common API. The report says which is which. So a pack is a list of mods, and today Horizon can bring over a part of that list. The coverage report is the honest answer for your pack. If two ported mods use the same namespace, the game can only load one of them. The launcher keeps the first, leaves the other off, and lists it under the pack. Measured on three packs: Vanilla Perfected (108 files) ports 2 mods, Slimes Adventure (105) ports 20, and All the Mods 10 (496) ports 42. Each opens a world, with no crash. Every ported mod is partial: its blocks, items, recipes and structures come over, its Java code doesn't. A world with All the Mods 10's 42 ported mods takes about 40 seconds to load, against about 5 without mods.

heading: Example: All the Mods 10
text: All the Mods 10 has 495 jars. Horizon's report sorts them: about 290 add content, 80 are libraries, and the rest are integrations, interface mods, tools and performance mods. A few dozen of the content mods carry over today. The measured numbers are in docs/modpacks.md .

heading: From the command line
text: horizon-launcher modpack list horizon-launcher modpack import <pack> horizon-launcher modpack port <pack> [--from <dir>] horizon-launcher modpack play <pack> horizon-launcher modpack remove <pack>

heading: Licences
text: Mods have their own licences, and Horizon respects them: it does not redistribute anyone's jars. The ports are made on your computer, from jars you downloaded, and stay there.

heading: Mods
text: Horizon has two kinds of mod: Content mods ( .hmod ) add blocks and items from data and assets: models, textures, recipes, loot tables, tags and structures, with no code. They work in single player today. This is also what the launcher's modpack carry-over produces. Native mods ( .hnmod ) are Rust code built into the game: a HUD, keys, commands, settings, new behaviour. Horizon's own Zoom, FPS Counter, Keystrokes and Minimap are native mods. They work in single player, on LAN and on servers (only what runs in your own game, on a server you join). Early. Reviewed mods are listed at playhorizon.dev/mods and on the launcher's Mods page. Content mods Install one from the launcher's Mods page (pick Horizon beside Modrinth), or put its .hmod file in the horizon-mods folder of the game folder (see Install for where that is). Open Options, Mods... . Each mod is listed with what it may do ("May add blocks and items to your worlds") and a switch. Content mods start off. Start the game again after a switch: content loads when the game starts. A mod that failed to load shows why, in red, on its row. Native mods A native mod is code, not sandboxed: it can do anything you can on your computer. So the launcher builds it into a game of its own, and only when you say so: Install it from the launcher's Mods page. The first time, the launcher says what native mods are and turns on Settings > Native mods (experimental) . There, press Build . The launcher names the mods and warns you in red; I trust these mods: build starts it. The first build downloads Rust and takes 20 to 30 minutes and a few GB of disk; later builds take a few minutes. Play the Native mods instance. It has its own worlds and options, so your other worlds never run the mods. In the game, Options > Mods lists each native mod with a switch and, when it has some, a Settings page and keys to rebind. Turn one off there and the next build leaves it out. Install only mods whose authors you trust. The registry lists a native mod only after a maintainer has read its source, and each one's page links it. Horizon's own mods say "Made by Horizon"; every other mod's page says who made it. Making a mod Make a mod is the full guide, for both kinds: the tools, your mod in the game, the hook points with a worked example, content mods, testing, and publishing on the registry . Java mod jars don't run in Horizon: their code calls and patches Minecraft's Java classes, and Horizon has none. What carries over is the data and assets inside a jar ( modpacks ).

heading: Finding resource packs and modpacks
text: The launcher's Mods page (launcher 0.17 and newer) searches Modrinth for what Horizon can load: resource packs and modpacks. Each result says how well it runs in Horizon ( Works , Partly , or Doesn't run ), and by default the page shows only what runs. Install downloads the file, checks it against the checksum Modrinth lists and refuses anything that does not match, then puts it in the right folder, with the packs it needs. Update and Remove are there too. A resource pack still has to be turned on in the game's Resource Packs screen. A modpack is imported on the Modpacks page . CurseForge support is coming soon: the page shows it, but doesn't search it yet. The same things work from a terminal: horizon-launcher mods search , install , update and remove .

heading: Java mods from the Mods page (next launcher release)
text: Java code does not run in Horizon, but much of what a mod adds is data: blocks, items, recipes, loot tables, tags, worldgen, textures. From the next launcher release, the Mods page also lists Fabric, NeoForge and Forge mods made for 26.3 and, before offering one, downloads its jar, checks it against Modrinth's checksum and reads it (without running it) to say what of it Horizon runs: Works : the mod is only content, and all of it carries over. Partly : its content carries over; the row lists what does not, such as machines and containers, mobs, blocks or items with behaviour of their own, recipe types of its own, or Mixins. Doesn't run : there is nothing to carry over (performance mods, libraries, mods that are all code). It is not offered. Install brings the mod over into horizon-mods and turns it on; start the game again to load it. Blocks take the closest vanilla block's shape, hardness and sounds, so a carried-over block can break faster or slower than in Java. Most popular mods today are Partly or Doesn't run : the verdict is the honest answer for each one.

heading: Data packs
text: A world's data packs go in its datapacks folder, as folders or .zip files with a pack.mcmeta , as in vanilla. Works today (single player and open-to-LAN worlds): Functions ( .mcfunction , with macros and line continuation), function tags (such as minecraft:load and minecraft:tick ), predicates and item modifiers . The /function , /datapack and /reload commands, and the choice of which packs are on, kept with the world. Not applied from data packs yet: custom recipes, loot tables, advancements and world generation. Horizon reads those from the vanilla data it prepared, and from content mods. Vanilla's own data is always on, and it matches vanilla: every command runs as vanilla does, and recipes, loot and world generation are checked against the real game.

heading: What Horizon does differently
text: Native code. Horizon is Rust, compiled for your system. There is no Java virtual machine, so no garbage-collection pauses and no warm-up while the code gets compiled as you play. It ticks what vanilla ticks, and no more. Mobs, minecarts and dropped items outside the simulation distance only check whether to despawn, as in vanilla. Before this was fixed, Horizon ticked seven times as many of them as vanilla at render distance 32. Work off the main thread. Chunks are generated, lit and meshed on worker threads, and unloaded chunks are written to disk in the background. Fewer, bigger draw calls. Terrain sections share one vertex arena and are drawn with one indirect multi-draw per pass. Mobs and block entities outside the view are skipped, and caves you cannot see into are culled. Distant terrain. The optional LOD distance draws terrain up to 1024 chunks away without simulating it. A server without Java. horizon-server is one native program. See below.

heading: The client
text: The numbers below are Horizon before and after a round of performance work, on an RTX 4080, in a fresh creative world flown over a village, a forest, the ocean and a mountain ( tools/graphics_bench.py ). They compare Horizon with an earlier Horizon, not with vanilla. Render distance 8 over a village: 363 to 2,409 FPS , and the slowest 1% of frames from 21.6 to 160.8 FPS. Render distance 16 over a village: 8 to 1,041 FPS . In a forest: 28 to 316 FPS. Render distance 32 improved too (a village went from 4 to 48 FPS) but still stutters in places : the slow frames are game ticks while chunks load, not drawing. The full tables, with the method and the Linux software-rendering run, are in docs/graphics.md . Horizon against vanilla. The benchmark exists: tools/perf_bench.py starts Horizon, vanilla 26.3 and vanilla with Sodium, Lithium, FerriteCore and ImmediatelyFast on the same machine, world, camera path and settings, and computes every number the same way. docs/benchmark.md says how it keeps the comparison fair. Its results for the client, measured on the project's own machines, are on the Benchmarks page , with the places where Java is faster. It also estimates other hardware from them, as a range, and shows players' uploaded results once at least three installs share a graphics card and processor. Measure your own computer. Horizon's half of that benchmark is built into the game. Close other heavy apps, plug in a laptop, and run in a terminal: horizon-launcher play --arg=--benchmark --arg=standard Add --arg=--render-distance --arg=16 to choose the render distance; your other settings are used as they are and stored in the report. The game creates its own world, horizon-benchmark (it never touches your saves), flies over a village, a forest, the ocean and a mountain, and quits by itself. --arg=village (or forest , ocean , mountain ) instead of --arg=standard flies one scene. For the run only, VSync is off and the frame rate unlimited; your options are not changed. The report is a .json file in the benchmarks folder of the game folder: System Folder Windows %APPDATA%\horizon\benchmarks macOS ~/Library/Application Support/horizon/benchmarks Linux ~/.local/share/horizon/benchmarks It holds startup times, each scene's chunk load time, the frame rate with its 1% and 0.1% lows, memory, and your machine (operating system, processor, memory, graphics card and driver). Its format is docs/benchmark-report.md . Share it. To add your computer to the Benchmarks page , either: upload it from the launcher: horizon-launcher data benchmark <the report's path> shows exactly what would be sent, without your file paths, and asks before sending. Or allow benchmark uploads once ( horizon-launcher data allow benchmarks ), and every later report is sent for you. See Privacy ; or post the .json file in the Discord.

heading: Servers
text: The latest bot benchmark compares horizon-server with vanilla 26.3, Paper and vanilla on Fabric with Lithium. It ran on a 4-thread laptop CPU (an i7-7500U), with 1 to 50 bots walking, exploring and standing around spawn, on another machine. All four servers did the same work. In short: Memory: 0.7 GB with one player and 1.1 GB with 50, against 3.4 to 4.5 GB for the Java servers (each with a 4 GB heap). That is 3.8 to 4.8 times less. Start: ready in 8 to 9 seconds, against 15 for vanilla, 17 for Fabric and 19 to 22 for Paper. CPU: from 10 players up, the least of the four. Average tick: Paper's was shorter at every player count, and Fabric with Lithium's at 1 and 10 players. Horizon's was shorter than vanilla's, and than Fabric's from 25 players up. Slow ticks: from 10 players up, Horizon's slowest ticks were the shortest of the four. 50 players: Horizon and Paper kept 20 TPS. Fabric with Lithium dropped to 17, and vanilla's watchdog stopped it. For more than 50 active players, give it more cores. The full report is benchmarks/server-four-way-2026-10-19 .

heading: Where else to look
text: Benchmark report format : what every benchmark writes. HORIZON_SPIKES=MS prints what made every frame slower than that many milliseconds slow; it is described in docs/graphics.md .

page: Control Horizon with your AI agent
heading: What an agent can do
text: Everything you can do with the mouse and keyboard, through commands instead of clicks: In the launcher: install, remove and prepare versions; start the game, alone or with a world, or a server; your settings and the extra game arguments; the mod browser (mods, resource packs, modpacks), imported modpacks and hosted servers; your accounts (names only), logs and crash reports, patch notes, the data collection settings and the benchmark. In the game: read what is on screen (every button, slider, field and slot, by name), click and type; move, look, mine, place, attack, use items and pick from the hotbar; the inventory, chests and every other container, crafting, trading, books and signs; every options page, including Horizon Settings, and any option by its key; worlds (create, open, rename, back up, delete), servers, LAN and Play with Friends; chat and commands, screenshots, F3 data, waiting for an event and the game's log. The full lists are in the repository: launcher commands and game commands .

page: Control Horizon with your AI agent
heading: Connect it from the launcher
text: The easiest way. Open the launcher's Settings and scroll to AI : Under Connect an AI agent , pick your client: Claude Code , Codex , Cursor or Any MCP client . For Claude Code and Codex, Add to Claude Code (or Add to Codex ) runs that client's own command to add Horizon. The command is shown above the button, and runs only when you click it. For the others, Copy the config and paste it into the file named above it. Test the connection starts Horizon's MCP server the way your client will and says how many tools it offers. Restart your agent if it was open, then ask it: "Say hello from Horizon". One server, called horizon , covers both the launcher and the game. Ask your agent to start the game and it starts it under its control. The game's tools are the ones whose names begin with game_ .

page: Control Horizon with your AI agent
heading: Copy-paste config
text: The launcher prints these with the exact path of your copy: horizon-launcher agent-config . The paths below are the usual ones: macOS: /Applications/Horizon.app/Contents/MacOS/horizon-launcher Windows: where you extracted the zip, for example C:\Horizon\horizon-launcher.exe Linux: where you put the AppImage or binary Claude Code , in a terminal: claude mcp add --scope user horizon -- /Applications/Horizon.app/Contents/MacOS/horizon-launcher mcp Codex , in a terminal: codex mcp add horizon -- /Applications/Horizon.app/Contents/MacOS/horizon-launcher mcp Or in ~/.codex/config.toml : [mcp_servers.horizon] command = "/Applications/Horizon.app/Contents/MacOS/horizon-launcher" args = ["mcp"] Cursor ( ~/.cursor/mcp.json ), Claude Desktop , and any other MCP client that takes the usual JSON: { "mcpServers": { "horizon": { "command": "/Applications/Horizon.app/Contents/MacOS/horizon-launcher", "args": ["mcp"] } } } The server talks over its standard input and output, so it needs no port and is never on the network.

page: Control Horizon with your AI agent
heading: A game you started yourself
text: A game your agent starts is under its control. A game you start with Play is not, unless you allow it. In the game, open Options , then Horizon Settings , then AI Agent... : Agent Control: On lets agents on this computer reach the game you started. It is off by default. The page shows whether an agent is connected and when it last sent a command. Copy Connection Details copies where the game listens, a command to try, and an MCP config for horizon-ctl , the game's own command line, which comes with the game. Turning Agent Control off disconnects agents at once.

page: Control Horizon with your AI agent
heading: The command line
text: The same commands, for scripts and terminals. --json prints JSON. See the versions: horizon-launcher versions Install the newest: horizon-launcher install latest Play a world: horizon-launcher play --world "My world" Change a setting: horizon-launcher settings install-new-versions on Find a resource pack: horizon-launcher mods search --kind resource faithful Read the game's log: horizon-launcher logs Turn No AI on: horizon-launcher no-ai on Start a game agents control: horizon-ctl launch --world Test See the game's state: horizon-ctl state See what is on screen: horizon-ctl ui Click a button by name: horizon-ctl click singleplayer Walk somewhere: horizon-ctl goto 10 64 -3 Take a screenshot: horizon-ctl screenshot shot.png horizon-ctl help lists every game command. horizon-launcher help lists the launcher's.

page: Control Horizon with your AI agent
heading: Safety
text: Your computer only. The launcher's server talks only to the agent that started it. The game listens on a local socket that only your user account can open; where there is none (Windows), it uses a localhost port and a secret token in a file only you can read. Nothing listens on your network. It asks before deleting. Removing a version, a modpack, a mod or a server, deleting a world or your collected data, and signing out need confirm: true from the agent. A call without it is refused and tells the agent to ask you first. It asks before reaching out. The tools that send something or reach other people say "only when the player asks". That covers joining a server, chatting on one, opening to LAN, hosting for friends, creating a server and sending data or a bug report. Data collection stays off until you allow it yourself. No secrets. No command returns your account tokens, session files or invite secrets. Accounts appear as names. Signing in stays a code that you enter in your own browser. Your agent, your rules. Clients such as Claude Code ask you before each tool they haven't been allowed to use. Allow only what you are happy for them to do.

page: Control Horizon with your AI agent
heading: No AI: turn it all off
text: In the launcher's Settings , under AI , turn on No AI . You can also use No AI in the game's Horizon Settings , or type horizon-launcher no-ai on . Then: the Connect an AI agent section and the game's AI Agent page are hidden; the game opens no control socket, even when it is started with one; horizon-ctl , horizon-ctl mcp and horizon-launcher mcp refuse with "AI features are off: turn off No AI in the launcher's settings"; the launcher's own commands (install, play, server, update and the rest) keep working, so scripts and packagers don't break. Turn it off the same way to bring everything back.

heading: Two kinds of mod
text: Content mod Native mod What it is Data and assets: blocks, items, recipes, loot tables, tags, models, textures, names, structures Rust code that hooks into the game: a HUD, keys, commands, settings, new behaviour File .hmod .hnmod Code None Rust, compiled into the game How players get it The game reads it when it starts The launcher compiles a game with it, in an instance of its own Safety Data only: it can't run anything Not sandboxed: it can do anything the player can on their computer Pick a content mod when what you add is a block, an item, a recipe or a structure: no compiler, and it works on every computer as it is. Content mods has the whole guide. Pick a native mod when the mod has to do something: draw on the screen, react to a key, add a command, change how the game plays. The rest of this page and the two after it are about native mods. A Horizon mod is not a Java mod. Fabric, NeoForge and Forge jars don't run in Horizon, and Horizon mods don't run in Java Minecraft. What carries over from a Java mod is its data and assets ( modpacks ).

heading: How a native mod works
text: A native mod is a bundle for horizon-mixins , a tool made for Horizon: a manifest, horizon-mixin.toml , and a few .rs files. Before the game is compiled, horizon-mixins adds your code to Horizon's own source and calls it from the places the manifest names. The result is an ordinary Horizon game with your mod built in. Horizon keeps a set of hook points for this: empty functions the game calls at fixed places (every tick, every frame, when it draws the HUD, when a key goes down, when the player types a command, when Options > Mods lists the mods), and helpers to read the player, draw text and keep settings. A mod that hooks only these builds on every later version of Horizon too, so it doesn't need a new release for each Nightly. Horizon's own Zoom, FPS Counter, Keystrokes and Minimap are made this way. Players never compile anything by hand. They install the mod from the launcher's Mods page, and the launcher compiles the game with it, with its own copy of Rust ( below ).

heading: The path
text: Set up (this page): the tools, the files of a native mod, and your mod in the game. The bundle : the manifest, what a mod builds on, and the .hnmod file. Hook points and helpers : what your code can hook and call, and a worked example. Content mods : blocks, items, recipes and textures from data files, with no code at all. Test it : unit tests, a check against Horizon's source, and the game with your mod in it. Publish it : package it and submit it to the registry.

heading: Install the tools
text: For a native mod you need: Rust , the stable toolchain, and Git . Python 3.11 or later, and rsync (on Windows, use WSL for the checks below). horizon-rust/horizon-mods , the registry's repository. Its native/tools/native.py applies your bundle to Horizon's source, checks and builds the game with it, and packages the .hnmod . It is what Horizon's own native mods use. The launcher , 0.2.23 or later ( Install ), with the game prepared at least once, to play with your mod. git clone https://github.com/horizon-rust/horizon-mods

heading: The files of a native mod
text: The guide's example, Playtime , shows how long you have played in a corner of the screen. Its folder: playtime/ ├── Cargo.toml runs the mod's unit tests: cargo test ├── compatibility.json the hook points it needs, and the commits it was tested on └── mixins/playtime/ ├── horizon-mixin.toml the manifest: its id, its version, what it hooks ├── runtime.rs the mod's own code: becomes the module crate::game::playtime ├── tick.rs one small helper for each hook it uses ├── hud.rs └── … Start from the example, or copy one of Horizon's own mods from horizon-mods' native/ folder : fps-overlay is the smallest. horizon-native-mod-template shows the other way, a mod that hooks one of the game's own functions instead of a hook point ( the bundle says what that costs).

heading: Check it against Horizon
text: From your clone of horizon-mods, give native.py the path to your mod's folder: cd horizon-mods python3 native/tools/native.py check /path/to/playtime It downloads Horizon's source at the commit your compatibility.json names (once), applies your bundle with horizon-mixins, and runs cargo check on the game. A mistake in your manifest is a horizon-mixins error; a mistake in your code is an ordinary Rust error, with the file and line. The first run compiles Horizon's dependencies and takes several minutes; later ones take seconds to a minute.

heading: See it in the game
text: The launcher builds a game with your mod from its folder: horizon-launcher native-build /path/to/playtime/mixins/playtime --trust-native-code It compiles the game with the launcher's own Rust and installs it in an instance named Native mods . Pick that instance in the launcher and press Play . The first build downloads Rust and takes 20 to 30 minutes; after a change to your mod, the next build compiles only what changed, a few minutes. --trust-native-code is the same decision the launcher asks players for in red: the mods run with full access to the computer. Build only code you trust.

heading: What players see
text: When a player installs a native mod from the launcher's Mods page, the launcher says once that native mods compile into a game of their own (the first build downloads Rust and can take 20 to 30 minutes) and turns on Settings > Native mods (experimental) . There the player presses Build , reads the red warning that names the mods, and builds with I trust these mods: build . The Native mods instance then plays the built game, with its own worlds and options. In the game, Options > Mods lists the mod with a switch and, when the mod has some, a Settings page and keys to rebind. A mod's settings live in horizon-mods/.horizon-mod-data/<id>/ in the game folder, one file per setting. Next: the bundle .

heading: The manifest
text: Playtime's mixins/playtime/horizon-mixin.toml , shortened to two hooks: [mod] id = "playtime" version = "0.1.0" priority = 100 # The commit it was tested on. [compatibility] horizon_revision = "6f8c7a0e5d531d3834c4d0be4659a1db8e7e5c2a" # runtime.rs becomes the module crate::game::playtime. [[module]] id = "runtime" file = "crates/horizon-client/src/game.rs" name = "playtime" source = "runtime.rs" [[injection]] id = "tick" kind = "HEAD" target = "horizon_client::game::native_hooks::Game<'_>::native_tick" helper = "tick.rs" bindings = [ { name = "game", ty = "&mut crate::game::Game<'_>", value = "&mut *self" }, ] [[injection]] id = "command" kind = "HEAD" target = "horizon_client::game::native_hooks::Game<'_>::native_command" helper = "command.rs" bindings = [ { name = "game", ty = "&mut crate::game::Game<'_>", value = "&mut *self" }, { name = "command", ty = "&str", value = "command" }, { name = "ran", ty = "&mut bool", value = "&mut *ran" }, ] Part What it is [mod] id The mod's id: a-z , 0-9 and _ . It names its row in Options > Mods, its settings folder and its keys. Keep it once you have published the mod. [mod] version Your mod's version, such as 0.1.0 . Each version you publish needs a new one. [mod] priority Orders the mods that hook the same function ( horizon-mixins' README has the rules). 100 , as Horizon's own mods, unless you need another. [compatibility] horizon_revision The Horizon commit the mod was made and tested on ( below ). [[module]] A file of yours added to the game as a module: source becomes crate::game::<name> . Your state, your logic and your tests go there. [[injection]] One hook: target is the function, kind where in it your code runs ( HEAD : first), helper the file with your code, and bindings what it receives. Helpers. A helper file holds one function, whose parameters are the bindings in order. Keep it short: read what the hook gives, call into your module, and write back what the hook asks for. Playtime's command.rs : // /playtime says it in chat; /playtime reset starts over. fn playtime_command(game: &mut crate::game::Game<'_>, command: &str, ran: &mut bool) { use crate::game::playtime as m; let Some(args) = command.strip_prefix("playtime") else { return; }; ... } A binding's value is an expression in the hooked function: &mut *self for the game, a parameter by its name. Module and helper files can't use inner attributes or //! comments, other files through mod or include! : use ordinary comments and inline modules. horizon-mixins refuses a bundle that breaks a rule, with the reason in one line. HEAD is enough for the hook points. horizon-mixins has other kinds ( RETURN , BEFORE_CALL , MODIFY_ARG , OVERWRITE and more) for hooking the game's own functions; its README lists them all.

heading: Hook points or a pinned commit
text: Horizon changes every day, and a hook names a function of its source. What a mod builds on depends on what it hooks: Only Horizon's hook points ( native_tick , native_hud and the others in hook points and helpers ). These keep their names and parameters from release to release, and new ones are only ever added. Each addition raises the hook points' version. Your mod names the version it needs, and the launcher builds it on the game the player plays, as long as that game has at least that version. This is the way to make a mod : it keeps working on new Nightlies without a new release. The game's own functions , such as Game::break_block . Those can change in any Nightly, so the mod builds only on the commit it pins in horizon_revision , a Nightly's. Every Nightly's commit is kept, so a pinned mod still builds after its Nightly is replaced, but the player plays that Nightly's game with it, and all the pinned mods of one build must pin the same commit. The launcher says which mod pins which when they don't.

heading: compatibility.json
text: native.py reads the mod's facts from compatibility.json , beside the mixins/ folder: { "game": "26.3", "hooks": 1, "horizon_repository": "https://github.com/horizon-rust/horizon", "horizon_revision": "6f8c7a0e5d531d3834c4d0be4659a1db8e7e5c2a", "horizon_mixins_repository": "https://github.com/horizon-rust/horizon-mixins", "horizon_mixins_revision": "0d6b103c70633d8fd9443d8d0acd3aadaacedb06" } Key What it is game The Minecraft version: 26.3 . hooks The hook points' version the mod needs. The current Nightly has versions 1 and 2 . horizon_revision The commit the mod was tested on: the same as in horizon-mixin.toml . Take a Nightly's ( Releases ). horizon_mixins_revision The horizon-mixins the mod was made with. Use the one Horizon's own mods use, in horizon-mods' native/ .

heading: The .hnmod file
text: What players install, and what you submit to the registry, is one .hnmod file: a zip holding horizon-native.json (the id, the version, the game, the commits and the hook points' version) and your bundle's .rs and .toml files, nothing else. The .hnmod is the source: the launcher compiles it on the player's computer, and a reviewer reads all of it before the registry lists it. native.py package makes it ( Publish ).

heading: What a native mod can do
text: Anything Rust can. A native mod is compiled into the game, so it isn't held to a list of permissions and nothing stops it from reading files or using the network. That is why players build native mods only after a warning, why the registry reviews every line, and why the launcher runs them in an instance of their own, with its own worlds and options. Keep your mod to what its page says it does. Next: hook points and helpers .

heading: Hook points
text: Each is a method of the game ( Game ), hooked with HEAD ( the bundle ). Bind game to &mut *self (or &*self for the two that take &self ) and the parameters by their names. Several mods can hook the same point: hooks that answer take an out parameter ( claimed , ran , zoom ), and a mod leaves it alone when another mod already set it. Hook point When the game calls it What you can do native_frame(elapsed: Duration) Once a frame, in a world or not Animate, time things native_tick() Once a tick (20 a second), in the window's game and, in single player, in its server's game too: check native_window() Count, update state native_hud(batch, corners) When the HUD is drawn (not under F1) Place a box with corners.place(corner, w, h) and draw it with native_fill and native_text native_key(key: &str, pressed: bool) A key or mouse button went down or up, by its vanilla name ( key.keyboard.z , key.mouse.left ). Keys come on any screen (check native_playing() ), mouse buttons while playing React to your keys native_wheel(steps: f32, claimed: &mut bool) The mouse wheel turned while playing Set claimed to keep the steps from the hotbar native_command(command: &str, ran: &mut bool) The player typed or clicked a command, without its slash, before the server sees it Run yours and set ran native_zoom(zoom: &mut Option<NativeZoom>) When the game sets the view's zoom (it applies while playing; the spyglass wins) Ask for a zoom: factor, smooth, mouse turning native_minimap(minimap: &mut Option<NativeMinimap>) When the game draws the minimap Ask Horizon's minimap to show: corner, size, scale, rotation, shape native_mods(mods: &mut Vec<NativeMod>) Options > Mods lists the native mods Push your row: id , title , description and your rebindable keys native_settings(mod_id: &str, buttons: &mut Vec<String>) Your settings page opens, and again after each click When mod_id is yours, push the labels of its buttons native_settings_click(mod_id: &str, button: usize) A button of a settings page was clicked When it is yours, change the setting and keep it Version 2 of the hook points adds one more, for the item panel and recipes .

heading: Helpers
text: Call them on game from your helpers: Helper What it gives or does native_on(id) -> bool Whether the player left your mod on in Options > Mods. Check it first in every hook: a mod turned off stays compiled in until the next build. native_playing() -> bool Playing, with no screen over the world. native_window() -> bool This game is the window's, not a server's. native_player() -> Option<NativePlayer> In a world: x , y , z , yaw , pitch and dimension . native_frame_rate() -> (u32, u32, u32) Frames in the last second, the slowest frame and the 1% low of the last 5 seconds, in frames per second. native_clicks() -> (u32, u32) Attack and use clicks in the last second. native_mapping(name) -> Option<(bool, String)> A vanilla control ( key.forward , key.jump , key.attack …): whether it is held, and its key as Controls shows it. native_mod_key(id, name, default) -> String The key the player chose for your key name in Options > Mods, else default ( key.keyboard.z ). native_corner_shown(corner) -> bool Whether a box in that corner shows: F3's debug screen takes the top left. native_text_width(text) -> f32 The width of a line of text, in GUI pixels. native_fill(batch, [x, y, w, h], argb) A rectangle on the HUD ( 0x78000000 is the box behind Horizon's own HUD text). native_text(batch, text, [x, y], rgb, shadow) A line of text on the HUD. native_chat(text) A chat line only this player sees. native_setting(id, key) -> Option<String> One of your settings: a file in your mod's folder, horizon-mods/.horizon-mod-data/<id>/<key> . native_set_setting(id, key, value) Keeps a setting. native_data_dir(id) -> PathBuf That folder, for anything else your mod keeps. Your own state lives in your module: a thread_local! for what changes, plain constants for the rest. The window's game runs on one thread, so its hooks see the same state; the single-player server's game runs on another and sees its own. Paths in helpers. Helpers are compiled inside the game, so they name your module crate::game::<name> , the hook points' types crate::game::native_hooks::… , and the HUD's horizon_client::hud::HudBatch , horizon_client::extras_hud::Corners and horizon_client::extras::Corner .

heading: The item panel and recipes (version 2)
text: Hook points version 2, in the current Nightly, add what a recipe viewer needs: the panel beside container screens ( native_panel_items , native_panel_recipes ), the hook native_panel_event for the player's clicks, searches and keys over it, and the game's items and recipes ( native_recipes , native_known_recipes , native_place_recipe , native_give ). The native port of Horizon's Recipes mod, in horizon-mods' native/recipes , uses them. A mod that uses them sets "hooks": 2 , and builds only on a Horizon that has them: the launcher builds it on the game the player plays when that game has them, else on the commit the mod was tested on.

heading: A worked example: Playtime
text: This mod counts how long you play, shows it in the top-right corner and keeps the count when you quit. /playtime says it in chat and /playtime reset starts over. Its settings page has one button, to hide the box. It hooks six points: native_tick , native_hud , native_command , native_mods , native_settings and native_settings_click . 1. The folder. Make the files from the setup page : Cargo.toml , compatibility.json and mixins/playtime/ . Cargo.toml makes runtime.rs a library, so cargo test runs its tests on your computer: [package] name = "playtime" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2024" publish = false [lib] path = "mixins/playtime/runtime.rs" 2. The mod's own code. mixins/playtime/runtime.rs holds the count and turns ticks into hours and minutes. It touches nothing of the game, so it is ordinary Rust: // Playtime: how long you have played, in a corner of the screen. This file is // both the mod's Cargo library (its tests run with `cargo test`) and the module // the bundle adds to the game as crate::game::playtime. use std::cell::Cell; pub const ID: &str = "playtime"; pub const VERSION: &str = "0.1.0"; thread_local! { // Ticks played; None until the saved count is read. static TICKS: Cell<Option<u64>> = const { Cell::new(None) }; } /// Ticks played: the saved count (`saved` reads it) the first time, then the /// running one. pub fn ticks(saved: impl FnOnce() -> Option<String>) -> u64 { TICKS.with(|t| { let n = t.get().unwrap_or_else(|| saved().and_then(|s| s.parse().ok()).unwrap_or(0)); t.set(Some(n)); n }) } pub fn set_ticks(n: u64) { TICKS.with(|t| t.set(Some(n))); } /// `1h 05m` from a number of ticks (20 a second). pub fn format(ticks: u64) -> String { let minutes = ticks / 20 / 60; format!("{}h {:02}m", minutes / 60, minutes % 60) } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { #[test] fn formats_hours_and_minutes() { assert_eq!(super::format(0), "0h 00m"); assert_eq!(super::format(20 * 60 * 65), "1h 05m"); } } 3. Count the ticks. tick.rs adds one tick in the window's game, while in a world, and saves the count once a minute: // Counts the ticks played in a world, and saves the count once a minute. fn playtime_tick(game: &mut crate::game::Game<'_>) { use crate::game::playtime as m; // Only the window's game counts: in single player the server thread ticks too. if !game.native_on(m::ID) || !game.native_window() || game.native_player().is_none() { return; } let ticks = m::ticks(|| game.native_setting(m::ID, "ticks")) + 1; m::set_ticks(ticks); if ticks % (20 * 60) == 0 { game.native_set_setting(m::ID, "ticks", &ticks.to_string()); } } 4. Draw the box. hud.rs asks corners for a place in the top-right corner, under any other mod's box there, and draws: // "Played 1h 05m" in a box in the top right corner, under the other mods' boxes. fn playtime_hud( game: &mut crate::game::Game<'_>, batch: &mut horizon_client::hud::HudBatch, corners: &mut horizon_client::extras_hud::Corners, ) { use crate::game::playtime as m; use horizon_client::extras::Corner; let shown = game.native_setting(m::ID, "shown").as_deref() != Some("false"); if !game.native_on(m::ID) || !shown || game.native_player().is_none() { return; } let text = format!("Played {}", m::format(m::ticks(|| game.native_setting(m::ID, "ticks")))); let w = game.native_text_width(&text) + 4.0; let (x, y) = corners.place(Corner::TopRight, w, 12.0); game.native_fill(batch, [x, y, w, 12.0], 0x7800_0000); game.native_text(batch, &text, [x + 2.0, y + 2.0], 0xFFFF55, true); } 5. The command. command.rs takes /playtime and leaves every other command alone: // /playtime says it in chat; /playtime reset starts over. fn playtime_command(game: &mut crate::game::Game<'_>, command: &str, ran: &mut bool) { use crate::game::playtime as m; let Some(args) = command.strip_prefix("playtime") else { return; }; if !game.native_on(m::ID) || !(args.is_empty() || args.starts_with(' ')) { return; } *ran = true; match args.trim() { "" => { let ticks = m::ticks(|| game.native_setting(m::ID, "ticks")); game.native_chat(&format!("You have played {}", m::format(ticks))); } "reset" => { m::set_ticks(0); game.native_set_setting(m::ID, "ticks", "0"); game.native_chat("Playtime reset"); } other => game.native_chat(&format!("Unknown option {other}: use /playtime or /playtime reset")), } } 6. Its row and its settings page. list.rs puts the mod in Options > Mods; settings.rs and click.rs make its page, with one button: // The mod's row in Options > Mods. fn playtime_listed(mods: &mut Vec<crate::game::native_hooks::NativeMod>) { use crate::game::playtime as m; mods.push(crate::game::native_hooks::NativeMod { id: m::ID.into(), title: format!("Playtime {}", m::VERSION), description: "How long you have played, in a corner of the screen.".into(), keys: Vec::new(), }); } // The mod's settings page: one button. fn playtime_page(game: &mut crate::game::Game<'_>, mod_id: &str, buttons: &mut Vec<String>) { use crate::game::playtime as m; if mod_id != m::ID { return; } let shown = game.native_setting(m::ID, "shown").as_deref() != Some("false"); buttons.push(format!("Shown: {}", if shown { "ON" } else { "OFF" })); } // A click on the settings page's button: show or hide the box, and keep it. fn playtime_click(game: &mut crate::game::Game<'_>, mod_id: &str, button: usize) { use crate::game::playtime as m; if mod_id != m::ID || button != 0 { return; } let shown = game.native_setting(m::ID, "shown").as_deref() != Some("false"); game.native_set_setting(m::ID, "shown", if shown { "false" } else { "true" }); } A mod with keys lists them in its row ( keys: vec![["zoom".into(), "Zoom key".into(), "key.keyboard.z".into()]] : the name, the label and the default), and the player rebinds them on its page; native_mod_key reads the choice. 7. The manifest. mixins/playtime/horizon-mixin.toml has the [mod] , [compatibility] and [[module]] parts from the bundle , and one [[injection]] for each helper.
