The bindings of the six: [[injection]] id = "tick" kind = "HEAD" target = "horizon_client::game::native_hooks::Game<'_>::native_tick" helper = "tick.rs" bindings = [ { name = "game", ty = "&mut crate::game::Game<'_>", value = "&mut *self" }, ] [[injection]] id = "hud" kind = "HEAD" target = "horizon_client::game::native_hooks::Game<'_>::native_hud" helper = "hud.rs" bindings = [ { name = "game", ty = "&mut crate::game::Game<'_>", value = "&mut *self" }, { name = "batch", ty = "&mut horizon_client::hud::HudBatch", value = "&mut *batch" }, { name = "corners", ty = "&mut horizon_client::extras_hud::Corners", value = "&mut *corners" }, ] [[injection]] id = "command" kind = "HEAD" target = "horizon_client::game::native_hooks::Game<'_>::native_command" helper = "command.rs" bindings = [ { name = "game", ty = "&mut crate::game::Game<'_>", value = "&mut *self" }, { name = "command", ty = "&str", value = "command" }, { name = "ran", ty = "&mut bool", value = "&mut *ran" }, ] [[injection]] id = "list" kind = "HEAD" target = "horizon_client::game::native_hooks::Game<'_>::native_mods" helper = "list.rs" bindings = [ { name = "mods", ty = "&mut Vec<crate::game::native_hooks::NativeMod>", value = "&mut *mods" }, ] [[injection]] id = "settings" kind = "HEAD" target = "horizon_client::game::native_hooks::Game<'_>::native_settings" helper = "settings.rs" bindings = [ { name = "game", ty = "&mut crate::game::Game<'_>", value = "&mut *self" }, { name = "mod_id", ty = "&str", value = "mod_id" }, { name = "buttons", ty = "&mut Vec<String>", value = "&mut *buttons" }, ] [[injection]] id = "click" kind = "HEAD" target = "horizon_client::game::native_hooks::Game<'_>::native_settings_click" helper = "click.rs" bindings = [ { name = "game", ty = "&mut crate::game::Game<'_>", value = "&mut *self" }, { name = "mod_id", ty = "&str", value = "mod_id" }, { name = "button", ty = "usize", value = "button" }, ] 8. Try it. cargo test runs the unit test. native.py check /path/to/playtime compiles it into the game, and horizon-launcher native-build builds a game you play ( how ). Open a world: "Played 0h 00m" sits in the top-right corner and goes up each minute. Type /playtime , then hide the box from Options > Mods > Playtime > Settings. Quit and come back: the count goes on from where it was. Where to go from here. Horizon's own mods are complete native mods to read, in horizon-mods' native/ : FPS Counter (a HUD box and its settings), Keystrokes (keys and controls), Zoom (a key, the wheel and native_zoom ) and Minimap. Next: content mods , or straight to testing .

heading: What a content mod is
text: A folder (while you work on it) or a .hmod file (to share it) holding a manifest, assets/ and data/ . Here is a mod that adds a ruby gem and a block of ruby: ruby/ ├── horizon-mod.toml ├── data/ruby/horizon/block/ruby_block.json the block: a template and what differs ├── data/ruby/horizon/item/ruby.json the item ├── data/ruby/recipe/ruby_block.json recipes, as in a data pack ├── data/ruby/recipe/ruby_from_ruby_block.json ├── data/ruby/loot_table/blocks/ruby_block.json what the block drops ├── data/minecraft/tags/block/mineable/pickaxe.json added to vanilla's tags ├── data/minecraft/tags/block/needs_iron_tool.json ├── assets/ruby/blockstates/ruby_block.json models and textures, as in a resource pack ├── assets/ruby/models/block/ruby_block.json ├── assets/ruby/models/item/ruby.json ├── assets/ruby/items/ruby.json ├── assets/ruby/items/ruby_block.json ├── assets/ruby/textures/block/ruby_block.png ├── assets/ruby/textures/item/ruby.png └── assets/ruby/lang/en_us.json the names players see

heading: The manifest
text: Every content mod has a horizon-mod.toml at its root: id = "ruby" name = "Ruby" version = "0.1.0" description = "A ruby gem and a block of ruby" authors = ["You"] api = "0.2" side = "both" capabilities = ["registries"] Key What it is id The mod's id: 1 to 64 characters of a-z , 0-9 and _ . It is the namespace of its blocks and items ( ruby:ruby_block ), and names its switch in Options > Mods. Keep it once you have published the mod. name The name players see. version Your mod's version, such as 0.1.0 . Each version you publish needs a new one. description One or two sentences for the Mods screen. authors A list of names. api "0.2" , the content format. side "both" . capabilities ["registries"] . Options > Mods shows it as "May add blocks and items to your worlds". namespaces Optional: more namespaces the mod's files use ( below ). Unknown keys are refused, so a typo is an error, not something silently ignored.

heading: Blocks
text: A block is a file data/<id>/horizon/block/<name>.json . It becomes the block <id>:<name> , with the template's behaviour, states and shapes: { "template": "minecraft:iron_block", "properties": { "hardness": 4.0, "light": 3, "sounds": "minecraft:amethyst_block", "map_color": 28 } } Key Meaning template The vanilla block it copies, such as minecraft:iron_block , minecraft:oak_door or minecraft:diamond_ore . A door copies a door's states and shape, an ore an ore's. properties.hardness How long it takes to mine (vanilla's destroy time; -1 cannot be broken). properties.explosion_resistance How well it stands up to explosions. properties.light The light it gives, 0 to 15. properties.requires_tool true : it drops nothing unless mined with the right tool (the tags say which). properties.friction How slippery it is (ice is 0.98 ). properties.map_color Its colour on maps, a vanilla map colour id from 0 to 61. properties.sounds A vanilla block whose sounds it uses. item false for a block with no item. By default the block gets an item of the same id. Every property you leave out is the template's.

heading: Items
text: An item is a file data/<id>/horizon/item/<name>.json , copying a vanilla item: { "template": "minecraft:diamond", "rarity": "uncommon" } It may change max_stack_size (1 to 99) and rarity ( common , uncommon , rare or epic , the colour of its name).

heading: Recipes, loot, tags, models and names
text: Everything else uses vanilla 26.3's own formats, so the Minecraft Wiki's pages on data packs and resource packs apply: Recipes in data/<id>/recipe/ , loot tables in data/<id>/loot_table/ . Tags : your own in data/<id>/tags/ . To add to vanilla's (which pickaxe mines the block, for example), put a tag file in data/minecraft/tags/ ; to add to the convention tags NeoForge and Fabric mods share, in data/c/tags/ . They add to the tag as a data pack does; "replace": true drops what came before it, and the log says so. Block states, models, item models and textures in assets/<id>/ , as in a resource pack. Models can use vanilla's parents, such as minecraft:block/cube_all . Names in assets/<id>/lang/en_us.json : "block.ruby.ruby_block": "Block of Ruby" , "item.ruby.ruby": "Ruby" . Structures. A content mod can also carry structures, template pools and structure sets in its namespace, and add its own pieces to vanilla's villages or to another mod's pools. The mod design page has the details.

heading: Namespaces
text: Your files go under your mod's id ( assets/ruby/ , data/ruby/ ), plus vanilla's and the convention tags ( data/minecraft/tags/ , data/c/tags/ ). Tags are the only files a mod may put under minecraft . A mod made from a Java mod whose files use other names lists them in its manifest: namespaces = ["kaisyn", "towns_and_towers"] . A listed namespace is the mod's own, as its id is, but blocks and items are still declared under data/<id>/horizon/ . minecraft , c and horizon can't be listed, and two mods that are on can't own the same namespace: the game keeps the first and logs the clash.

heading: Limits
text: A mod's files use vanilla's resource-name characters: at most 65,536 files, 16 MiB each and 512 MiB in all. A file the game can't read (a block model that doesn't parse, a recipe with a typo) is logged and skipped, as vanilla does: the rest of the mod still loads. Read the log while you work. Unknown keys in a block or item file are refused, and the mod stays off with the reason on its row. Content mods work in single player today. Playing them together on a server is planned.

heading: Start one
text: Install cargo horizon-mod , the tool that makes, builds and checks content mods. It needs Rust to install, and builds from source in a few minutes; run it again later to update it: cargo install --git https://github.com/horizon-rust/horizon cargo-horizon-mod cargo horizon-mod new my-blocks --template content makes a content mod with one block, Glowing Amethyst: an amethyst block that gives light, with its block state, model (using vanilla's amethyst texture), item model, name, loot table, a recipe (an amethyst block and glowstone dust) and the pickaxe tag. Rename and copy its files to add your own.

heading: Try it and share it
text: While you work, give the game the folder as a dev mod , always on: in the launcher's Settings , put --dev-mod "/path/to/ruby" in Game arguments , then press Play (clear it when you are done). With a horizon-client you built yourself, cargo horizon-mod run --game <path> builds the mod and starts that game with it. The first start with a new set of mods takes a little longer while the game adds their content to its tables; after a change to the files, start the game again. To share it, build the .hmod in the mod's folder: cargo horizon-mod build cargo horizon-mod check target/horizon-mod/ruby.hmod build checks the files as the game will and packs the manifest, assets/ and data/ into target/horizon-mod/<id>.hmod , with no compiler involved. check reads it as the registry does and says "no code: content only, nothing to run". Players put that file in their horizon-mods folder and turn it on in Options, Mods... , and you can publish it like any mod. A content mod has no code. For behaviour (a HUD, a command, a key), make a native mod ; it can come beside a content mod that holds its blocks and items. Next: test it .

heading: Unit tests for your logic
text: Code that doesn't call the game (formatting, maths, parsing a command's arguments) is ordinary Rust in your module. Keep it there, keep the helpers thin, and test it with #[test] , as Playtime does with its format function. The mod's Cargo.toml makes the module a library, so the tests run on your computer, with no game: cargo test

heading: Check it against Horizon
text: From your clone of horizon-mods : python3 native/tools/native.py check /path/to/playtime python3 native/tools/native.py check /path/to/playtime --horizon latest check downloads Horizon's source at the commit in your compatibility.json , applies your bundle with horizon-mixins and runs cargo check on the game, with warnings as errors. It fails when the source has fewer hook points than your mod needs, when horizon-mixins refuses the bundle (a wrong target or binding, with the reason in one line), and on any Rust error in your code. --horizon latest does the same on the newest Nightly, and --horizon <commit> on any commit: run it when a Nightly comes out, to know your mod still builds before players find out. Several mods at once, as a player's set is built: python3 native/tools/native.py check /path/to/playtime zoom fps-overlay

heading: In the game
text: python3 native/tools/native.py build /path/to/playtime builds the game with your mod (Horizon's fast profile) and prints where it is. Start it with --resources pointing at prepared game files: each version the launcher installed has them in its .local/horizon-client/26.3 folder. Or build with the launcher, as players do, and play the Native mods instance: horizon-launcher native-build /path/to/playtime/mixins/playtime --trust-native-code Things to try each time: Options > Mods : your row, its switch and its settings page. Turn the mod off: it must do nothing until it is on again. Every command, with no arguments, with good ones and with wrong ones. The title screen and a world, single player and a server: native_player() is None outside a world, and in single player the server's game ticks too. Quitting and starting again, for a mod that keeps settings. F1 (no HUD) and F3 (the debug screen takes the top-left corner). A native mod runs inside the game, so a panic in your code stops the game. Use Option and Result for what can go wrong, as the helpers do.

heading: Content mods
text: Start the game with your mod as a dev mod ( how ) and read the log ( logs/latest.log in the game folder): a file the game can't read is logged and skipped. After each change to the files, start the game again. Things to try: Each block: place it, mine it with and without the right tool, and look at what it drops. Each recipe in a crafting table or furnace, and in the recipe book. The names and textures, in the inventory and in the world.

heading: Check it as the registry does
text: Before you publish, run what the registry runs on every submission, on the file you will submit: cargo horizon-mod check target/horizon-mod/ruby.hmod cargo horizon-mod check native/target/playtime-0.1.0.hnmod It reads the file's manifest and checks its contents: a content mod's files as the game will read them, a native mod's bundle without running anything. It also checks modpacks ( .hpack ) and resource packs ( .zip ). --json prints the report as JSON, for scripts. --key <public key> --signature <file>.minisig also checks your signature ( Publish ). A file that passes check passes the registry's automatic checks. A person still reviews it, and for a native mod reads all of its code ( Publish ). Next: publish it .

heading: Before you submit
text: Choose a version. Set version in the manifest ( horizon-mod.toml for a content mod, horizon-mixin.toml for a native mod), such as 1.0.0 . Every version you publish needs a new one, and a published file never changes. Make the file. A content mod: cargo horizon-mod build writes target/horizon-mod/<id>.hmod . A native mod: package it . That file is what you submit. Check it. cargo horizon-mod check <file> must pass ( Test a mod ). Publish the source. Put the mod's source in a public repository, under a licence that lets players use it (MIT, Apache-2.0, GPL and so on, as an SPDX name). Reviewers read it, and the file must be made from it.

heading: Package a native mod
text: From your clone of horizon-mods : python3 native/tools/native.py check /path/to/playtime python3 native/tools/native.py package /path/to/playtime package writes native/target/<id>-<version>.hnmod and prints its size and SHA-256. It holds horizon-native.json , made from your compatibility.json , and your bundle's .rs and .toml files. horizon-mixin.toml and compatibility.json must name the same Horizon commit: package refuses the mod when they don't. The same files always give the same .hnmod , so anyone can make it again from your source and compare. Before you submit a native mod, build it on the Horizon players play: native.py check --horizon latest for the newest Nightly ( Test a mod ).

heading: Sign it
text: Signing is optional and recommended. When your project has a public key, every later version must be signed with the matching secret key, so nobody else can publish an update in your name, even with access to your GitHub account. Horizon uses minisign signatures. Install minisign ( brew install minisign , scoop install minisign , or your Linux distribution's package), then make a key pair once: minisign -G -p horizon-mods.pub -s horizon-mods.key Keep horizon-mods.key and its password private and backed up: losing it means changing the project's key by hand, through the registry's maintainers. The public key is the last line of horizon-mods.pub (it starts with RW ). Sign each file you publish, and check the signature as the registry will: minisign -S -s horizon-mods.key -m native/target/playtime-0.1.0.hnmod cargo horizon-mod check native/target/playtime-0.1.0.hnmod --key "RW…your public key…" --signature native/target/playtime-0.1.0.hnmod.minisig The report then says "signature verified".

heading: Submit it
text: Open playhorizon.dev/mods/submit and sign in with GitHub. The page reads only your public profile. Then fill in: The file : the kind (mod or native mod), the .hmod or .hnmod , its id (the manifest's id ), its version, the Minecraft version (26.3) and what changed. Its page : the name, a one-line summary for the list, a description (Markdown), the authors, the licence, the source address and, optionally, a square PNG icon (at most 256 KiB). Signature : your public key (for a new project) and the file's .minisig . Submit for review checks the file again and opens a pull request in horizon-rust/horizon-mods . It adds mods/<id>.toml , with you as the project's owner. The repository's checks run cargo horizon-mod check on the file again and post their report on the pull request.

heading: Review and publication
text: A reviewer reads the pull request, your source and the checks' report. For a native mod, the .hnmod is the source: a maintainer reads every line of it, since it runs with the player's rights, and its description should say what it does and what it doesn't. Questions and requests for changes come as comments on the pull request: answer them there, and submit a new version from the form when the file must change. When the reviewer merges it, the file becomes a release of horizon-mods within minutes, and the project gets its page at playhorizon.dev/mods/<id> and shows in the launcher. The page shows your source, licence and the file's SHA-256; a native mod's page says it is code the launcher compiles, with no sandbox. Players install a native mod from the launcher's Mods page, and the launcher compiles the game with it after a warning that names it.

heading: Updates
text: An update is the same form with a new version: it adds the version to your project's entry. The project's owners publish updates of a content mod without a reviewer's extra look; every version of a native mod is read again. If the project has a key, the new file must be signed with it. Without the form, you can open the pull request by hand: the horizon-mods README says how. The registry's file formats are in the mod index reference .

heading: Reports and takedowns
text: Anyone can report a project from its page ( Report it ). A project that does harm is taken down: the launcher then refuses its files and turns installed copies off, telling players why.

heading: What the levels mean
text: Stable : only additions within a major version. A change that would break you comes as a new major, served beside the old one for at least 180 days. Preview : documented and tested. It may change at a new line (0.1 to 0.2), after a deprecation of at least 30 days during which old and new both work. Experimental : opt-in only, and it may change in any release. Every API has its own version (the native hook points are version 1, the server's control API is /api/v1 ), separate from the game's release number. The whole policy: stability and versioning .

heading: How they are designed
text: Each API starts from what its users need to do, and from how Horizon is built: Rust, wgpu and a server thread that runs every world. Horizon's APIs are its own: they are not modelled on another mod loader's, renderer's or server platform's. Vanilla Minecraft 26.3 is the reference for game concepts such as ids, commands and data packs. They are safe by default (content mods are data only, native mods build only after a warning and play in a game of their own; control sockets only listen on your computer, behind a token) and cost nothing when unused.

heading: References that can't drift
text: Each reference is written by code from the source it describes, and a test fails when the two differ: horizon-ctl and the launcher from their command tables, the server from its settings template and route table. A change to an API changes its reference in the same pull request.

heading: Horizon APIs
text: Horizon has seven surfaces that other programs and people build on. Each one has an API (the contract: what you may call, read or write, and what Horizon promises about it) and an SDK (the tools that help you use it). This section has one page per surface, plus the rules every surface follows: stability and versioning . heading: How these APIs are designed
text: From the people who use them. Each API starts from what a mod author, a pack author, a server host or an agent needs to do, written down as tasks ("a host backs up the world from a script"), and from how Horizon is built: Rust, wgpu and a server thread that runs every world. A function exists because a task needs it. Our own design. Horizon's APIs are not modelled on any other project's. Contributors may know other mod loaders, renderers and server platforms exist, but their source and API references are never read, copied or paraphrased here, and our names, shapes and docs are not taken from theirs. Vanilla Minecraft 26.3 is the reference for game concepts: ids, commands, server.properties , data packs and resource packs. Safe by default. A content mod is data and runs no code; a native mod runs with the player's rights, so it is off by default, behind a warning and reviewed before the registry lists it; the control sockets listen on this computer only, behind a token; nothing here is on by default where it would change vanilla's look or behaviour. Free when unused. An API nobody uses costs nothing per tick or per frame: no engine, no thread, no allocation. One contract for every mode. In-frame single player, the server thread, LAN and the dedicated server run the same gameplay code ( AGENTS.md ), so a server-side API serves all of them.

heading: References are generated
text: A reference page is written by code from the source it describes, and a test fails when the two differ: Page Generated from Update it with server-reference.md horizon-server 's help, config::TEMPLATE , api::ROUTES HORIZON_WRITE_DOCS=1 cargo test -p horizon-server reference horizon-ctl-commands.md the command table in crates/horizon-client/src/bin/horizon-ctl/commands.rs horizon-ctl help --markdown > docs/horizon-ctl-commands.md launcher-commands.md launcher/src/cli.rs HORIZON_WRITE_DOCS=1 cargo test --manifest-path launcher/Cargo.toml the_launcher_reference launch-reference.md crates/horizon-client/src/game/launch_api.rs HORIZON_WRITE_DOCS=1 cargo test -p horizon-client --lib launch_api So a pull request that changes an API also changes its reference, and the reviewer sees the API's diff in the reference's diff. The guides (overview, how-to, examples) are written by hand.

heading: Each surface's page
text: Every page has the same parts: Overview (what you can build), Guide (where to start), Reference , Examples , Stability (the level of each part, per stability.md ), Changelog and Not there yet (what is planned, so nobody builds on a guess). The website shows these pages at playhorizon.dev/docs/api , built from this folder, and a summary for players and authors at playhorizon.dev/docs/apis (in the website's repository, horizon-rust/horizon-site).

heading: Versions
text: Each API has its own version , separate from the game's release ( v0.2.14 , versioning.md ) and from Minecraft's. A game release says which API versions it serves. Semantic versioning , MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH . A line is what stays compatible: 0.1 , 0.2 , … before 1.0, then 1 , 2 , …. Before 1.0: an addition makes the next patch ( 0.1.0 → 0.1.1 ); a breaking change starts the next line ( 0.2.0 ). From 1.0: an addition makes the next minor ( 1.0 → 1.1 ); a breaking change starts the next major ( 2.0 ). Where the version lives: API The version A user names the line they need Content mods the manifest's api line api = "0.2" in horizon-mod.toml Native mods the Horizon and horizon-mixins revisions the bundle pins horizon_revision in horizon-mixin.toml Agent control the control protocol's version ( hello replies it; MCP serverInfo carries the release) horizon-ctl --api 0.1 (planned) Server control API the path ( /api/v1/ ) the path server.toml the file's keys; a key is never renamed in place nothing: old files keep loading Launcher commands the command names and their --json output nothing Data formats a version or schema field in the file the reader rejects versions newer than it knows

heading: What counts as a breaking change
text: Breaking: removing or renaming anything; changing a type, a default, a unit or a meaning; making something optional required; refusing input that was accepted; a JSON field that changes type. Not breaking: a new function, interface, capability, command, endpoint, tool or server.toml key; a new optional argument or JSON field (readers must ignore fields they don't know); faster, or fixing behaviour to what the reference already says.

heading: Stability levels
text: Every part of an API has one level, shown in its reference and its surface page. Experimental Preview Stable Who may use it opt-in only (a flag or a manifest field naming it); never in a release default anyone; marked "preview" where players see it (a mod's row on the Mods page) anyone May change in any release, without notice only at a new line, after a deprecation only at a new major, after a deprecation Deprecation window none at least 30 days, with one release line serving old and new at least 180 days, with the old major served beside the new one Needs a design note a generated reference, a guide section, an example, compatibility tests the same, plus one line of real use without a break Promotion. Experimental → preview when it has what the table asks. Preview → stable when real users (a published mod, a host's script, an agent's tool) used it for a whole line and nothing broke. The maintainers' orchestrator proposes the promotion with the evidence (the compatibility tests, the complete docs, that line of use) and Ludovic approves it. Horizon-only by design. An API is stable only for what Horizon itself does; a vanilla concept it exposes (a block id, a command, a server.properties key) changes when vanilla changes it, with a version port ( version-ports.md ), and the changelog says so.

heading: Deprecation and removal
text: The pull request that deprecates marks it where it is defined (a /// Deprecated: use X; goes in 0.3. doc comment, a deprecated field in a tool's schema) and adds the replacement in the same release. The reference shows it as deprecated, and the surface page's changelog says what replaces it and when it goes. Using it logs one warning per mod, session or client, naming the replacement; it keeps working. It is removed only after the window, and only at the next line (preview) or major (stable). A line or major that is no longer served is refused with a clear message ( needs API 0.1; this Horizon serves 0.3 and 0.4 ), never loaded half-way.

heading: Compatibility tests
text: Every preview and stable API has tests that run old users against the current code, in CI: API The test Content mods the content template builds and checks with cargo horizon-mod , and mod_content 's tests load content mods; a line is served as long as they pass Native mods hook points are only ever added, and tests keep each one hookable ( tests::hook_points_stay_hookable and tests::loot_table_load_stays_hookable , game/native_hooks.rs ) Agent control a transcript per protocol version: commands and the reply keys each must have Server api::ROUTES against route() (generated reference); a server.toml from each release line parses to the same settings; golden replies per endpoint Launcher the generated reference; golden --json output per command Launch the generated reference, which holds --launch-api 's reply; every listed option is accepted; horizon-prepare 's --progress json lines ( progress_json_lines_keep_their_shape ), its --launch-api reply and options ( launch_api::tests , launch_api_options_are_in_the_help ) Data formats a sample file of every version a reader accepts, read by today's reader The generated references are the API's own diff: a pull request that changes an API changes its reference, and the reviewer applies the rules above to that diff.

heading: Changelog
text: Each surface page ends with a changelog: one line per change, newest first, with the API version and the pull request. Deprecations and breaking changes are in bold. The release notes of the game release that ships a change link it.

heading: The registry index and .hpack
text: Horizon's registry lists what is made for Horizon and reviewed: content mods ( .hmod ), native mods ( .hnmod , native-mods.md ), modpacks ( .hpack ), resource packs and Horizon shader packs ( .hshader , shaders.md ). A project is listed by a reviewed pull request in horizon-rust/horizon-mods that links its GitHub repository; its versions are the repository's GitHub releases, read and checked by the registry's CI with no pull request and no review per version. The launcher and the website read one file, index.json , which that repository's CI builds. The Rust types and every check below are horizon_mods::index and horizon_mods::modpack (feature index ); the sample is crates/horizon-mods/tests/index/index-v1.json , read by the tests with the files it lists. Level: preview ( stability.md ). Schema 1.

A reader refuses a higher number with "update Horizon" rather than misread it. projects[].id [a-z0-9_]{1,64} , unique; a mod's is its manifest's id . kind mod (content), native-mod , modpack , resourcepack , shader (Horizon's own shader packs, not Iris or OptiFine packs). Other kinds (data packs, worlds, themes) may come without a new schema: a reader keeps a kind it doesn't know and doesn't offer it. summary , description One line for lists; Markdown for the project's page. owners GitHub logins allowed to publish updates. license , source An SPDX expression and an https:// address of the source code: both required. icon https:// , optional. key The author's minisign public key. When set, every version must be signed with it; an update signed with another key is refused. Absent: the project is unsigned and the launcher says so. versions Newest first, at least one. downloads How many times its files were downloaded, every version together: GitHub's count of each release asset, summed by the publish job, which runs every hour. Absent until a file is downloaded. Read-only: never in an entry. api A mod's API line (its manifest's api ); a native mod's pinned revisions ( native-1/<horizon>/<mixins> ); a modpack's manifest format ( 1 ). side , capabilities A mod's, read from its manifest by CI, never typed by hand. api_level A legacy field in old entries; the launcher ignores it. game The Minecraft version it is for. requires A modpack's mods: { id, version, sha256 } , each a version in this index with that hash. file A plain name with the kind's extension ( .hmod , .hnmod , .hpack , .zip , .hshader ), an https:// URL (the registry's release https://github.com/horizon-rust/horizon-mods/releases/download/<id>-<version>/<name> , or an asset of the project's own repository, https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/download/<tag>/<name> : the launcher accepts exactly these shapes), the size (at most 64 MiB), the lowercase hex SHA-256, and the .minisig text when the project has a key. revoked Files taken down: one file by sha256 , or every version of id without it. The launcher refuses to install them and turns installed copies off with the reason. Readers ignore fields they don't know, so an optional field can be added to schema 1. Renaming or removing a field, or changing what one means, makes schema 2.

heading: Before a file is installed
text: index::check_file runs on the downloaded file, before it reaches the game folder: Its size and SHA-256 are the ones the entry lists, and it isn't revoked. With a project key: its signature verifies with that key (minisign's prehashed and legacy signatures both). What the file says matches the entry: a mod's horizon-mod.toml (id, version, API, side, capabilities), its API level when the entry lists one, and its content's fence ( mods.md ); a native mod's horizon-native.json and horizon-mixin.toml (id, version, the pinned Horizon and horizon-mixins revisions); a modpack's manifest (id, version, format, game, mods); a resource pack's pack.mcmeta ; a shader pack's horizon_shader_api::check and manifest (id, version, shader API). A kind this build can't install is refused with "this Horizon can't install a … yet".

heading: .hpack
text: A zip holding horizon-modpack.toml and, optionally, overrides/ . The mods are not inside: the launcher downloads each from the index and checks it as above. format = 1 id = "cozy" # [a-z0-9_]{1,64}: the profile's folder name = "Cozy" version = "1.0.0" description = "Coordinates and a calm render distance." authors = ["Horizon"] game = "26.3" [[mods]] id = "coords_hud" version = "0.1.0" sha256 = "e1135345692f6dd8fd4c51920151944b82333e17049c9bb7d756f27b8deefc53" on = true # optional, default true: turned on in the profile's horizon-mods.txt Unknown keys are refused. overrides/ may hold only options.txt , horizon-graphics.txt , horizon-extras.txt , resourcepacks/<name>.zip and horizon-mods/.horizon-mod-data/<a listed mod>/... (a mod's own saved settings, a native mod's saved settings), each at most 64 MiB and 256 MiB in all; anything else refuses the pack. The launcher copies them into the profile's game folder.

heading: The registry repository
text: horizon-rust/horizon-mods holds one mods/<id>.toml per project and revoked.toml . An entry is a link and a page : the project's GitHub repository and what the listing says about it. Its versions are the repository's GitHub releases. What an entry can't vouch for is read from the file by the kind's own check ( index::inspect ): a mod's API, side and capabilities, a modpack's mods, the size. Types and rules: horizon_mods::index::registry . id = "coords_hud" # the file's name, and the manifest's id kind = "mod" # mod | native-mod | modpack | resourcepack | shader repo = "horizon-rust/coords-hud" # GitHub owner/name: its releases are its versions owners = ["ludovic111"] # GitHub logins responsible for the project key = "RWT..." # optional: the minisign public key every version is signed with icon = "icons/coords_hud.png" # optional: a PNG of at most 256 KiB in the repository, or https:// # The page. Each field may instead come from horizon-registry.toml in the repo (below); these win. name = "Coordinates HUD" summary = "One line, at most 160 characters." description = """Markdown.""" authors = ["Horizon"] license = "MIT" # source defaults to https://github.com/<repo> Versions come from the releases. For each entry with a repo , the registry's CI lists its GitHub releases (drafts and pre-releases are skipped) and, for each release it has not read yet, downloads the asset with the kind's extension (and its <name>.minisig when the project has a key), runs the checks of a submission (below), and if they pass adds the version. The version, the game and the pins are the file's own manifest ( horizon-mod.toml , horizon-native.json , horizon-modpack.toml , the shader manifest); the release's tag stands in where the file names none (a leading v is dropped). published is the release's date, changelog its notes (cut at 6000 characters), file.url the asset's address in the repository, file.sha256 and size are computed by the CI and, when GitHub gives the asset a digest, must equal it. Tags and asset names use letters, digits, . , - , _ and + . A release that fails a check is skipped and reported in an issue of the registry; the same bytes are not read again. The versions that passed are kept, in the order they were read, in versions/<id>.json on the registry's versions branch (the page last read from the repository is kept with them), so the history is auditable and the index does not change when a repository does: a release deleted or an asset replaced later does not change the index (the launcher refuses bytes that are not the pinned ones). horizon-registry.toml at the root of the repository, as of the newest release's tag, may hold name , summary , description , authors and license (unknown keys, and anything about owners, key, kind or icon, are refused): they fill the page fields the entry leaves out. A listing that is incomplete without it is refused until it is. [[versions]] in an entry are optional and kept for projects listed before releases were read, and for Horizon's own mods built in the registry ( native/<name>/ ): [[versions]] # newest first version = "0.1.0" # letters, digits, '.', '-', '_': the release tag is <id>-<version> published = "2026-10-24" game = "26.3" file = "coords_hud-0.1.0.hmod" # the name players download, a release asset of the registry sha256 = "e113..." # pins the reviewed file signature = """untrusted comment: ...""" # when the project has a key changelog = "" # optional The index lists both kinds, newest first. A project listed by its repository with no release yet is not in the index. # revoked.toml [[revoked]] id = "bad_mod" sha256 = "1111..." # optional: without it, every version reason = "Sent chat messages it didn't declare." date = "2026-10-24" Who reviews what: a project is reviewed when it is listed (the pull request that adds its entry: the repository, its source, the page, the owners), and again if its repo , owners or key change. Later releases are checked automatically, not reviewed by a person ; revoked.toml takes a bad one down. A signing key makes a stolen repository or account useless for publishing an update. The submission form's service ( crates/horizon-mod-registry ) lists a new project: it signs the creator in with GitHub, reads the repository's address and the page, and opens the pull request. It no longer takes updates for a project listed with a repo : "publish a GitHub release in <repo>". Projects without a repo can still be updated through the form (it uploads the file to the repository's staging release as <sha256>.<extension> and opens a pull request; an owner's update with nothing else changed is merged by owner-update once the checks pass). An owner may turn a mod into a native-mod once by sending an .hnmod (reviewed by hand, never an owner update); no other kind change goes through. A submission that GitHub broke off after making its submit/<id>-<version> branch can be sent again: the same account's retry starts that branch again from main while it has no open pull request; anyone else's is refused. Unknown keys in an entry are refused. Its CI runs cargo-horizon-mod ( crates/cargo-horizon-mod ): Command What it does cargo horizon-mod check <file> [--json] A submission's checks: its kind's (above) and its signature with --key and --signature . It runs no mod's code: a native mod's source is read by the reviewers when it is listed. cargo horizon-mod registry check <base> <head> --files <dir> check on each hosted file head lists and base doesn't: a pull request's new files. cargo horizon-mod registry list <checkout> <sha256> <id> <version> <file> per hosted version: the files to download. cargo horizon-mod registry build <checkout> --files <dir> --out index.json Reads every entry, its hosted files ( <dir>/<sha256> ) and versions/<id>.json , lists every problem, and writes the index ( --release , ending in / , defaults to the repository's releases, for hosted versions). cargo horizon-mod registry release <checkout> <id> <file> --tag T --published D [--notes F] [--signature F] [--game G] The checks of a submission, then the version a release of the project's repository is, as the index lists it (JSON). cargo horizon-mod registry page <checkout> <id> <horizon-registry.toml> The repository's page file, checked against its entry (JSON). cargo horizon-mod registry review <base> <head> --author <login> A pull request's changes: a published file never changes and is never removed (take it down in revoked.toml ), a kind never changes; changes by a non-owner and to owners, keys or the repository are pointed out for the reviewers. How the repository runs (its workflows are in .github/workflows/ ): A pull request ( check.yml ) runs registry review , downloads each new hosted file from the staging prerelease, runs registry check on it and builds the index it would publish; the report is the run's summary. The tool is cargo-horizon-mod from Horizon at the commit in the repository variable HORIZON_REV . Every hour, and on a push to main ( publish.yml ): read the new releases of every entry with a repo as above and keep the result on the versions branch, make each new hosted version a release <id>-<version> , and deploy index.json and icons/ to GitHub Pages: https://horizon-rust.github.io/horizon-mods/index.json , served with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * . Merging an entry needs the check run and a CODEOWNER's review. Weekly , cleanup.yml deletes staged copies of published files after 7 days and of files no open pull request lists after 30. Taking a file down is a pull request adding it to revoked.toml . Removing an entry outright (a test, a project nobody installed) fails registry review on purpose and needs an administrator's merge. Kinds open to submissions: mod (content only), native-mod , modpack , resourcepack , shader . A shader pack ( .hshader ) passes horizon_shader_api::check , the check the game runs before it loads one ( horizon-shader check , shaders.md ): every stage validated by naga and translated for Vulkan, Metal and DirectX 12; its manifest's id, version and shader API line are its facts. heading: Guide
text: horizon-server init in an empty folder, then horizon-server start ( hosting.md ). From a script: horizon-server status --json , horizon-server cmd say hi , horizon-server backup . By hand: horizon-server console attaches to the running server (live log, status header, command line). From an AI agent: horizon-server --dir /srv/minecraft mcp is an MCP server on stdio with a tool per endpoint ( players , ban , events , set_config ...); add it to the agent's MCP servers, run as the server's user. From a program: read .horizon/api.json (address and token), then GET /api/v1/status with Authorization: Bearer <token> . A program that runs elsewhere or keeps its settings (a Discord bot) uses a fixed address and token: [api] bind and [api] token in server.toml ( hosting.md ). Moderate: horizon-server players , horizon-server ban NAME [REASON] , or POST /api/v1/players/ban . An action runs vanilla's console command on the running game, so it kicks, logs and saves banned-players.json exactly as an operator's /ban does; the reply says whether anything changed and has the console's lines. Monitor: point Prometheus (or any scraper that sends a bearer token) at GET /api/v1/metrics/prometheus . Watch: GET /api/v1/events with Accept: text/event-stream streams what happens as server-sent events: every log line ( log ), the supervisor's phase , and the game's typed join , leave , kick , chat and death events with the player's name and UUID ( ?types=chat,death picks some). Last-Event-ID (or ?since=N ) resumes after a reconnection; without Accept: text/event-stream it answers the events after since as JSON. A tool written for vanilla: turn on vanilla's management protocol ( management-server-enabled = true in [properties] , hosting.md ); it answers as vanilla 26.3's does, and rpc.discover describes it. A tool that speaks RCON (a hosting panel, a Discord bridge): turn on enable-rcon with a password in [properties] ( hosting.md ); a command runs as one typed in the console. A tool that reads the GS4 query (a server list, a status page): turn on enable-query in [properties] ( hosting.md ); it answers the MOTD, the version and the players over UDP.

heading: Overview: what a shader author will be able to do
text: Write WGSL against documented stages of Horizon's renderer, with typed inputs, options the player can change, a reload as soon as a file is saved and an overlay that shows what each pass costs and draws. The renderer keeps everything that makes it fast (culling, batching, LOD, the mesher); a pack changes how surfaces and light look, not how the world is fed to the GPU.

heading: The design
text: A pack is a folder or a zip with horizon-shaders.toml (id, name, version, the api line, the stages it uses, its options) and WGSL files. No preprocessor and no other shading language: WGSL is what wgpu validates and compiles for Vulkan, Metal and DirectX 12. Stages, not pipelines. A stage is a function with a fixed signature that the renderer calls inside its own pass, for example a terrain material ( fn material(input: TerrainInput) -> Surface ), the lighting of the visible surfaces, the sky, an optional shadow pass, and a chain of full-screen post passes ending in the frame. A pack that leaves a stage out gets vanilla's look for it. Typed inputs. Each stage receives structs (the frame: time, camera, sun and moon, weather, fog; the surface: position, normal, block and its light) whose WGSL is generated from the Rust types the renderer uploads. The generated reference lists every field with its unit and range, and a test fails when it drifts. Options are WGSL override constants. The manifest declares each option (on/off, a number in a range, a choice) with its default; the game shows them on the pack's settings screen and sets them when it builds the pipeline. No text substitution, and every option combination is validated the same way. Hot reload. The game watches the pack's folder. A saved file is validated with naga and the stage rebuilt; on an error the last good version keeps drawing and the error, with its file and line, is shown in the overlay. Debug overlay. GPU time per stage and pass (timestamp queries), the targets each pass writes (show any of them full-screen), the pack's options and its compile errors. Budgets. A pack declares the targets and passes it needs; the renderer refuses more than its limits, and the benchmark ( benchmark-report.md ) records the pack and its cost, so "fast" stays measured. Off by default. Without a pack the renderer is vanilla's look, and no pack code runs.

heading: The pack format (schema 1)
text: A pack is a folder, or the same files zipped as a .hshader , with horizon-shaders.toml at its root (crate horizon-shader-api ; the sample with every key is crates/horizon-shader-api/tests/samples/schema-1/ ): schema = 1 # the manifest's format; a reader refuses schemas newer than it knows id = "soft_light" # [a-z0-9_]{1,64}: the settings key and the registry id name = "Soft Light" version = "1.0.0" api = "0.1" # the shader API line the WGSL is written for description = "..." # optional, like authors and license shared = ["common.wgsl"] # optional: WGSL put before every stage's file, in order [sky] # each stage is optional, but a pack has at least one file = "sky.wgsl" clouds = true # optional: false when the pack draws its own clouds sun = true # optional: false when the pack draws its own sun (the moon stays) stars = true # optional: false when the pack draws its own stars [material] file = "material.wgsl" files = ["pbr.wgsl"] # optional, on any stage: WGSL put after `shared`, before this stage's file fog = false # optional: the pack fogs its surfaces itself (Horizon does when absent or true) [vertex] # needs [material]: where corners of terrain are drawn, for the world and the shadow map; shares the material's module file = "vertex.wgsl" [weather] # the colour of rain and snow streaks file = "weather.wgsl" [shadow] # optional, needs [material] or [[post]]: a shadow map from the sun (the moon by night) resolution = 2048 # its side in texels, 256 to 8192 distance = 128.0 # half the side of the square it covers, in blocks, 32 to 512 solid_materials = [10] # optional: [[materials]] ids drawn into the map whole, cutouts ignored [[post]] # full-screen passes, in the order they run (8 at most) file = "post/grade.wgsl" name = "Colour grade" # optional: the GPU time overlay's label output = "bloom" # optional, not on the last pass: writes this target, read by name in later passes scale = 0.5 # optional, with output: 1, 0.5 or 0.25 of the world's size [[options]] # 64 at most; `id` is the WGSL `override` it sets id = "saturation" name = "Saturation" type = "float" # bool, float (min, max, step), int (min, max), choice (values) default = 1.1 min = 0.0 max = 2.0 step = 0.05 [[materials]] # 1024 at most: MaterialInput.material, the first entry that matches id = 10 # 1 to 65535; 0 is a sprite no entry names sprites = ["block/*_leaves"] # sprite names, any number of * each blocks = ["oak_log", "grass_block:snowy=true"] # optional: the sprites these blocks' models draw with, where no entry's sprites name them translucent = false # optional: this id's sprites draw in the translucent pass, clear texels and all [[pages]] # optional: the options page's layout, the first the one it opens on id = "main" name = "Sample" items = ["page:colour", ""] # a button opening a page, an empty slot (or an option's id) [[pages]] id = "colour" name = "Colour" # the page's title and its button's label description = "How colourful the picture is." # optional: the button's tooltip columns = 1 # optional: 1 or 2 (default) buttons a row items = ["saturation"] [[textures]] # 8 at most: a PNG every stage reads as noise and noise_sampler id = "noise" file = "noise.png" filter = "linear" # optional: linear (default) or nearest wrap = "repeat" # optional: repeat (default) or clamp [[lights]] # 256 at most: block_light_color's colour, the first entry that matches color = [0.3, 0.7, 1.0] # each channel 0 to 4 blocks = ["soul_*"] # block names, any number of * each [[particle_lights]] # 32 at most: these particles join the frame's coloured lights particles = ["firefly"] # names, `firefly` or `minecraft:firefly`; the first entry naming one wins color = [0.8, 0.9, 0.4] # each channel 0 to 1; the particle's alpha is its intensity reach = 4.0 # blocks, 0.25 to 16; the 16 nearest lights shine, read by MaterialInput.colored_light [[tags]] # 32 at most: bit i of MaterialInput.tags is the i-th tag id = "glass" sprites = ["block/glass", "block/*_stained_glass"] # sprite names, at most one * each [budget] gpu_ms = 1.5 # optional: the GPU time the pack aims to add (0 to 16 ms) [reflection] # optional, needs [material]: when the water mirror (`reflection`) is drawn option = "reflections" # optional: drawn while this option is not 0 (else whenever the material reads it) An option's override has the type of its kind: bool , f32 , i32 , or u32 for a choice (the index of the value). The pack holds only the manifest, the .wgsl files it names (each used, UTF-8, 256 KiB at most), README.md , LICENSE ( .md , .txt ) and icon.png , under plain paths, 8 MiB in all. A .hshader is built the same way every time (files in path order, fixed dates), so a pack's SHA-256 depends only on its files.

heading: Contribute
text: Horizon is open source and takes pull requests. The one rule that shapes everything: it plays exactly like vanilla. Wherever vanilla has a feature, vanilla is the specification. Questions and ideas are welcome on Discord . Bugs and feature requests go in GitHub issues . If you want to take something on, say so in its issue so nobody else starts the same work.

heading: The repository
text: github.com/horizon-rust/horizon holds the game and the launcher, plus the tools, tests and docs that build, check and release them. This website is built in a separate repository; its API pages come from the game's docs/api/ . crates/ is the game, as Rust crates: the client, the server, the world and protocol code, the mod system, the design tokens and more. launcher/ is the launcher, a GPUI app with its own Cargo workspace. tools/ holds the parity harness drivers, the parity runner, the release tools and the self-check. tests/ holds the Python tests, benchmarks/ the published results and packaging/ the installers. docs/ holds the developer documentation, indexed here : the native client, the design system, world generation, the parity workflow, the release flow and more.

heading: Build it
text: You need Rust (stable), Python 3.10 or newer, JDK 25 and, on Linux, the ALSA and udev headers ( libasound2-dev libudev-dev ). Horizon never downloads the game: it prepares its resources from your own copy of Minecraft 26.3. git clone https://github.com/horizon-rust/horizon.git cd horizon cargo run --release -p horizon-prepare -- --prepare --server-jar ~/Downloads/server.jar cargo run --release -p horizon-client Everything prepared lands in the git-ignored .local/ . It is derived from the game: never commit it or share it. The launcher is its own workspace: cd launcher && cargo run . The website builds with node build.mjs in website/ .

heading: Parity harnesses
text: A harness is a tools/test_*_parity.py script. It drives the same inputs through Horizon and through the vanilla client and server bytecode from your own copy of the game, and checks that the outputs are identical. There are 281 in the audit. Read the vanilla code before writing Horizon's. tools/rea_vanilla.py queries the pinned game bytecode, for example python3 tools/rea_vanilla.py method net.minecraft.world.level.block.DispenserBlock dispenseFrom . Say in your pull request which vanilla classes and methods you followed. Gameplay changes come with a harness , new or extended, so the next change cannot silently break them. Copy a nearby one. python3 tools/parity.py runs the harnesses a change can affect. The parity workflow explains the rest. Horizon's own features (the launcher, the new menus) follow the design system and stay off by default wherever they would change the vanilla look. Everything players run is Rust. Python and Java are fine for dev tools and harness drivers, never for player-facing code.

heading: How pull requests are checked
text: Self-check first. Run python3 tools/pr_ready.py and paste the block it prints into your pull request. It runs rustfmt, clippy with warnings denied, the tests of the crates you touched, the Python tests, the public-tree check and the harnesses your change can affect. verify runs on every pull request on GitHub's Linux runners: the same checks, without the vanilla harnesses. Docs-only changes finish in seconds. parity runs the affected harnesses on a maintainer's computer, which holds the game files. It never runs a fork's code on its own: a maintainer reads the change, then adds the run-parity label, which runs it once on your current commit. Small pull requests. One change each, under about 500 lines of code where you can. They get reviewed and merged the same day. Labels. feature when players get something new, skip-release when they see no change, nothing for a fix. We set them if you cannot. "Allow edits by maintainers." Tick it. When something small is left, we push the fix ourselves instead of sending you back. Every merge to main that players can see is released automatically, so main always stays playable. See the release flow .

heading: What never goes in
text: Never commit game files, decompiled source or prepared resources. tools/check_public_tree.py rejects them, and git config core.hooksPath .githooks runs it before every commit. Tracked Java is allowed only under the project's own dev/horizonlab namespace. CONTRIBUTING.md is the short version of this page, and the contributors are listed on the home page.

heading: Do I need to buy Minecraft?
text: Yes. Horizon contains no Minecraft code, assets or data. It builds its game files from your own copy of Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3, on your computer. See Install .

heading: Is Horizon official?
text: No. It is not an official Minecraft product, and it is not approved by or associated with Mojang or Microsoft. It is open source, under the MIT licence.

heading: Is Horizon the same as Minecraft Rust Edition?
text: "Minecraft Rust Edition" is a name some players use for Horizon, because Horizon is Minecraft: Java Edition rewritten in Rust. It is not an edition made by Mojang or Microsoft. Other projects use the name too, including a fork of Horizon. The original is the one on this site, with its source at horizon-rust/horizon . See What Horizon is .

heading: Will my Forge, NeoForge or Fabric mods work?
text: No. Java mod jars do not run in Horizon. Horizon has its own mod system, and the launcher can carry over the data-and-assets part of some Java mods. See Modpacks and Mods and data packs .

heading: Can I join public servers?
text: Not yet. Most public servers check that you own Minecraft, which needs a Microsoft account sign-in, and Horizon cannot do that yet. It can join servers in offline mode, such as your own or a friend's. See Multiplayer .

heading: When will Microsoft sign-in work?
text: We cannot give a date. It needs an app registration with Microsoft and an approval from Mojang that the project does not have yet. Until then, this site only describes what works today.

heading: Can vanilla players join my Horizon world or server?
text: Yes. A vanilla 26.3 client can join a Horizon server and a Horizon LAN world. See Multiplayer and Host a server .

heading: Can I use my existing worlds?
text: Yes. Worlds from Minecraft 1.8 to 26.2 are upgraded the way vanilla upgrades them, and saves use vanilla's format. Copy your world into the game folder's saves folder, and make a backup first, as you would before opening a world in any new version.

heading: Where are my worlds and settings?
text: In the game folder: ~/.local/share/horizon on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/horizon on macOS and %APPDATA%\horizon on Windows. Updating the game never touches it.

heading: Does it change my normal Minecraft install?
text: No. Horizon only reads your Minecraft files when it prepares, and keeps what it needs in its own folder.

heading: Why does preparing need Java 25?
text: Preparation runs vanilla's own data generator on your copy of the game, to read data such as every item's default components, and that is Java. It is needed for the preparation only. The game and the server themselves run without Java.

heading: What does "100% vanilla parity" mean?
text: Every subsystem matches vanilla in every harness that compares it. It means 100% of what the harnesses compare, not proof that nothing else differs. See What Horizon is and the status table .

heading: Which systems does it run on?
text: Linux x86-64, macOS on Apple Silicon and Windows x64. See supported systems .

heading: Are shader packs supported?
text: Not right now. They have been removed, and will come back later, written again from scratch. See Settings .

heading: Does Horizon collect data?
text: Only if you say yes, and each kind has its own switch. Everything is off by default. The one thing sent without asking is an anonymous "I'm playing" ping, for the count of how many play right now: it holds a random number made each time the game starts, the version, your OS and whether a world is open to LAN, and nothing about you. See Privacy .

heading: How often does it update?
text: Often. Every change players can see is released automatically after it is merged, so new versions can come out several times a day. Each one is tested before it goes out (the game has to start and draw a world), and the launcher installs it as soon as it is out. There is one version for everyone. See Install .

heading: What do the version numbers mean?
text: Since 0.2, every release has a number: 0.2.0, then 0.2.1, 0.2.2 and so on, one for each release. The game and the launcher are both on 0.2 and count on their own, so you can play Horizon 0.2.7 with launcher 0.2.3. A bigger step, such as 0.3, is announced when it comes. Releases before 0.2 were named after the day they came out (2026.10.19.15); every 0.2 release is newer than all of them.

text: See Logs, crashes and bug reports .
